AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

On-chain data indicates the attacker behind the $6.3 billion Binance theft depositing about $4 million into three Binance deposit addresses.

At the same time, Binance's first post-hack reserve snapshot reveals its biggest assets covered with buffers as small as 2.7 ETH and $6 of USDT. Binance's full zero-knowledge proof of those figures is due by Tuesday.

Some of the money stolen from Binance has started going back to Binance.

Blockchain intelligence firm Arkham has flagged the entity it tracks as "Binance Hacker" depositing about $4 million into three Binance deposit addresses. Arkham states those addresses "likely represent nested service(s)." These are third-party exchanges that use Binance for liquidity and custody, giving their own customers deposit addresses that sit on Binance's infrastructure.

If Arkham is right, the hacker isn't depositing into an ordinary Binance account. The money would be going to smaller platforms that operate through Binance. Exchanges have long known this is a weak point for stolen funds moving into normal trading. Either way, Binance is now receiving stolen funds at its own deposit addresses while it works to show customers it has replaced what was taken.

The FBI has attributed the October 29 theft to North Korea. The deposits come at a sensitive moment. Binance has just published its first reserve snapshot since the hack and has promised a full cryptographic proof of it by Tuesday.

$4 million is a small slice of a theft worth about $6.3 billion, but it matters for two reasons.

It reveals how the laundering works. Nested services are a common way into the regulated financial system. A third-party platform that relies on Binance for custody may run weaker identity checks on its own owners. Funds deposited there can be swapped and withdrawn without the hacker ever opening a Binance account.

Binance can act on it. Binance can't freeze bitcoin and ether sitting in wallets nobody controls, and it doesn't control the stablecoins that issuers like Tether and Circle have frozen. Deposits that land at its own addresses are different: they are on Binance's platform, so Binance can freeze them itself. One of the first tests of how Binance handles the money still in the hacker's hands is whether it freezes these funds and identifies the services that own the addresses.

While the hacker's funds move, Binance has been rebuilding its reserves. Its proof-of-reserves page now shows:.

Industry observers note that the first page covers Binance's six largest assets. Customer balances are what users hold. Reserves are on-chain wallet balances, including assets held with outside custodians.

The second page has four more assets, and two of them stand out:.

Sources indicate that why USD1 and RLUSD matter: these are two of the stablecoins whose issuers froze stolen funds after the attack. World Liberty Financial froze $27 million of USD1, and Ripple began freezing RLUSD the same night. Both now show reserves above what Binance owes customers.

Assets with outside custodians: part of several reserves sits with outside custodians rather than in Binance's own exchange wallets:.

Asset | Held with third-party custodians.

The striking part isn't that the ratios reach 100%. It's how closely they stop there.

Compared with October's report: Binance's previous monthly report, published in early October before the hack, showed BTC at 100.35% and USDT at 103.88%. ETH was already at exactly 100.00%. After the theft:.

According to recent reports, not every asset is that tight. USDC, ZEC and BNB carry buffers of 1.3% to 6%. The thinnest buffers are in BTC, ETH, USDT and SOL, which are among the assets the attacker took in the largest amounts.

How Binance states it got here: the pattern fits Binance's account of replacing the stolen assets in stages. It reported 80% replaced on Friday, 90% on Saturday and 95% on Sunday. The remaining 5% is in less-liquid tokens it is still buying. The money came from:.

Binance confirmed taking 7,499 BTC from SAFU and has pledged to refill the fund to about $1 billion.

In a recent development, what the snapshot can't show: it was taken a little over a day after the theft, once the rebuild was under way. It demonstrates the balance sheet after the replacement, not how large the gap was on October 29.

Binance indicates the full proof takes 40 to 50 hours to compute. Its latest enhancement says it will be ready "by Tuesday, 2026-11-03 (UTC)." The system is open source, in Binance's zkmerkle-proof-of-solvency repository.

What the proof guarantees, according to the project's circuit design document:.

In a recent development, the design also guards against a "dummy user attack" identified by Ethereum Foundation researcher Enrico Bottazzi. In that attack, fake accounts holding cheap tokens are used to offset debts in major assets.

Recent findings suggest that what it doesn't prove: the reserve side. The project's verifier config describes the totals as information "published by CEX, it represents CEX's liability." The reserve figures are checked a different way, against the wallet addresses Binance publishes through the page's "Download All Address" option.

What customers can do: each user can get a Merkle proof for their account and check it against the published root. They can use the verifier code in Binance's repository rather than Binance's own interface. That doesn't prove Binance is solvent, but it confirms the user's balance was counted.

Binance has rebuilt its reserves to 100% across its ten largest assets, but on several of them the buffer is only a few coins. Meanwhile, stolen funds are reaching its deposit addresses through platforms that run on its infrastructure. Tuesday's proof can confirm customer balances. It can't show how Binance handles the stolen money arriving at its own door.

Here’s who’s getting the richest from Anthropic’s $81 billion IPO

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Anthropic’s seven cofounders are each worth about $20 billion on paper after the company’s record-breaking IPO on Thursday, which also made thousands of its employees and some Silicon Valley investors extremely rich.
  • Dario and Daniela Amodei, as well as the other cofounders—Tom Brown, Jack Clark, Jared Kaplan, Sam McCandlish, and Chris Olah—have all pledged 80% of their personal Anthropic equity to philanthropic causes.
  • Industry observers note that the company behind the popular AI chatbot Claude debuted on the Nasdaq Thursday, initially raising $81.3 billion in a public offering that surpassed the previous record of $75 billion SpaceX’s IPO initially brought in over the summer.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Anthropic’s seven cofounders are each worth about $20 billion on paper after the company’s record-breaking IPO on Thursday, which also made thousands of its employees and some Silicon Valley investors extremely rich.

Dario and Daniela Amodei, as well as the other cofounders—Tom Brown, Jack Clark, Jared Kaplan, Sam McCandlish, and Chris Olah—have all pledged 80% of their personal Anthropic equity to philanthropic causes. These commitments, though, are voluntary and not legally binding, according to Anthropic’s IPO filing.

Industry observers note that the company behind the popular AI chatbot Claude debuted on the Nasdaq Thursday, initially raising $81.3 billion in a public offering that surpassed the previous record of $75 billion SpaceX’s IPO initially brought in over the summer. On Friday, Anthropic unveiled that underwriters had purchased millions more shares, bringing the offering’s total to about $93.5 billion.

Sources indicate that after pricing its shares at $83 apiece on Wednesday, the firm opened trading significantly higher and closed out the day at around $97. Despite shares falling to $85 on Friday afternoon amid a broader tech-fueled stock retreat, the company is still worth around $1.1 trillion—surpassing the market cap of Walmart.

Industry observers note that the record IPO is great news for the cofounders and insiders who have been supporting Anthropic since it was founded in 2021. The biggest gains, though, belong to Amazon and Google, whose stakes are worth about $316 billion combined—more than twice the roughly $142 billion held by the seven cofounders. Here are some of the people and companies who stand to benefit the most.

According to recent reports, anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and his sister, Anthropic’s president and chair of the board, Daniela Amodei, are among the figures most commonly associated with the manufacturer. But there are another five cofounders who are cashing in as well.

Industry observers note that each of its seven cofounders owns between 237 million and 241 million shares after the offering. At the stock’s price of about $85 on Friday, that means each founder has holdings worth approximately $20 billion, putting them (at least on paper) in the same league as Bridgewater Associates founder Ray Dalio, who has a net worth of $21 billion, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index.

Each founder also sold approximately 3.38 million shares in the IPO, worth about $280 million at the offering price.

According to recent reports, despite owning a minority of the company’s equity, Anthropic’s cofounders control 50.1% of its shareholder voting power. The nearly equal distribution of shares among the seven founders is unusual for a Silicon Valley startup, Fortune reported.

Besides its cofounders, some Silicon Valley investors are also set to win substantial. Lightspeed Venture Partners, an early backer of Snapchat, led a $3.5 billion funding round in Anthropic in March 2025 when the company was valued at $61.5 billion. The VC firm owns less than 2% of the company, according to Bloomberg, yet its stake is still reportedly worth tens of billions of dollars.

Other VCs like Menlo Ventures also own a stake representing less than 2% of the organization, Bloomberg reported. Iconiq has invested more than $6 billion in Anthropic since 2025, and its stake is worth more than $26 billion, the outlet reported. Anthropic in total has more than 400 venture investors, according to PitchBook, yet no VC firm owns more than 5%, Fortune reported.

In a recent development, the manufacturer’s historic IPO means even some smaller stakes are now worth billions. Sound Ventures, the venture firm cofounded by Ashton Kutcher, invested about $435 million in Anthropic and owns about 0.5% of the company, Bloomberg reported. It’s unclear, though, how much Kutcher himself benefited from the trade as the actor best known for his role on That ’70s Show stepped down as general partner at the firm earlier this year.

Former Google CEO Eric Schmidt also owns about 1% of Anthropic, according to Bloomberg, putting his stake’s value at about $11 billion at Friday’s share price.

Recent findings suggest that one early investor who won’t be reaping the rewards is FTX founder Sam Bankman-Fried, who is serving a sentence of 25 years in prison after being convicted on fraud and conspiracy charges. Bankman-Fried has appealed his sentence to the Supreme Court. The trading firm he founded, Alameda Research, invested $500 million in Anthropic, but FTX’s bankruptcy estate sold most of its stake in 2024 to repay creditors. Among the buyers was Bankman-Fried’s former employer Jane Street, which stands to reap a multibillion-dollar windfall.

Many of the firm’s roughly 5,300 employees are also getting rich thanks to generous stock-based compensation. Private-markets research firm Sacra estimated that 2,800 current and former employees could hold at least $1 million in pretax vested equity in the company at a $1.35 trillion valuation, Reuters reported.

Industry observers note that some of the earliest employees stand to benefit disproportionately. At least 400 early hires could hold equity worth $100 million or more, according to CNBC.

To be sure, it’s hard to estimate which employees hold how much stock because Anthropic’s IPO filing discloses aggregate equity awards but not their distribution among individual employees.

Now that Anthropic is public, non-founder employees are allowed to sell up to 10% of certain holdings, and up to another 35% following the release of Anthropic’s 2026 financial results.

Some of the biggest gains from the company’s IPO will go to two Massive Tech giants, Amazon and Google. Anthropic’s IPO filing estimated that Amazon would own 14.6% of the company’s outstanding shares and Google would own 13.4%.

Recent findings suggest that amazon’s stake stems from billions of dollars in investments the tech giant has made in Anthropic dating back to 2023, around the time it had just 160 employees. At the time, Amazon committed an initial $1.25 billion as part of a deal to ultimately invest $4 billion in Anthropic. In exchange Anthropic agreed to make Amazon Web Services its primary cloud provider for critical workloads and make Claude available to AWS customers.

In total, Amazon invested $8 billion in convertible notes between 2023 and 2025 and put in another $10 billion in preferred stock in 2026.

Google has also poured billions into Anthropic, including $10 billion it invested in a financing round earlier this year and another $10 billion in a private placement alongside the IPO.

At the company’s roughly $85 per share stock price Friday, Amazon’s 1.94 billion shares would be worth about $165 billion, while Google’s 1.77 billion shares would be worth around $151 billion.

Industry News: The 5 Little Habits That Made a Bigger Difference in My Business Than I Expected

  • When people talk about growing a business, they usually focus on the big moves: landing a major client, launching a latest service or hiring the right team.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

When people talk about growing a business, they usually focus on the big moves: landing a major client, launching a latest service or hiring the right team. But when I look back at my own journey, some of the things that helped me most were much smaller and easier to overlook.

According to recent reports, ralph Waldo Emerson once wrote, “The first wealth is health.” I didn’t fully appreciate that until I saw how much my energy, focus and decisions depended on how well I took care of myself. That’s why I’m starting with the health habits that changed how I work, before moving on to the habits tied directly to running my business.

None of these were clever strategies or big investments. They were simple habits I built into my everyday routine. On their own, each one seemed minor. Over time, together, they made a real difference. Here are the little habits that I personally believe helped my business the most.

Industry observers note that one of the simplest habits that made a surprisingly major difference in my business was walking every day. When I first started spending long hours behind my laptop, I could easily go through an entire day barely moving. Eventually, I realized that waiting for free time to exercise wasn’t working, so I decided to make walking part of my daily routine.

Recent findings suggest that the more I thought about it, the more I noticed how many people around me had the same problem. Founders, freelancers, marketers: Most of us spend our days at a desk and tell ourselves we’ll be more active once work slows down. But that moment rarely comes, and the effects build up quietly. According to Okdermo, about 41.9% of American adults are affected by obesity. There are many reasons behind that number, but a lack of daily movement is one of them, and it’s something I could actually control. I didn’t want my work to slowly become the reason my health got worse. Walking was the easiest way I found to change that, and I didn’t have to rebuild my whole schedule to do it.

And it turns out that you don’t need an extreme daily step count to see meaningful health benefits. According to Solace, walking 7,000 steps a day was associated with a 47% lower risk of death from any cause compared with walking 2,000 steps. Personally, I aim for around 15,000 steps a day, not because I believe it’s some magic number, but because I’ve noticed that I feel better, sleep more soundly and think more clearly when I reach it. Everyone should find a daily step count that works for their own body and lifestyle rather than blindly following someone else’s target.

Sources indicate that over time, my walks have also become some of the most productive parts of my day. I listen to podcasts, think through ideas and sometimes even take calls and meetings while I walk. I record voice memos and jot down notes whenever something useful comes to mind. Walking and talking at the same time helps me let go of stress, but more importantly, it clears my head. Some of my best business decisions were made not at my desk, but halfway through a walk.

Business impact: Walking helps me clear my mind, solve problems faster and make better business decisions.

Industry observers note that walking was a great start, but I knew I needed more than daily steps to stay in good shape. The problem was that I used to skip workouts whenever work got busy. There was always another deadline or client who needed my attention. That’s why I decided to hire a personal trainer. I knew that having someone waiting for me would make it harder to find excuses.

And it worked. According to PersonalTrainers, 88.2% of people training with in-person supervision met their workout attendance target, compared with 52.2% of those training on their own. Having someone hold me accountable made all the difference.

Now I treat workouts like client meetings. I put them on my calendar and rarely cancel. I’ve learned that sometimes the best way to stay consistent is to make a commitment to someone other than yourself.

Business impact: Working with a trainer helps me stay disciplined, manage my schedule better and maintain the energy I need to run my business.

Recent findings suggest that taking care of my health gave me more energy and focus, but some of the habits that made the biggest difference were directly tied to how I run my business. One of them was giving more attention to existing clients instead of constantly chasing latest ones. Early on, I was so focused on winning new projects that I sometimes overlooked the people who were already paying for my services. Eventually, I realized that building long-term relationships was far more valuable than constantly starting from scratch.

I began listening more carefully, communicating more openly and looking for ways to deliver more than clients expected. The results have been worth it: Today, clients stay with my business for an average of 3.5 years. And the financial value of retention shouldn’t be underestimated. According to Coruzant, even a 5% improvement in customer retention can increase profits by 25% or more. For me, that reinforces why taking better care of existing clients deserves just as much attention as bringing in newly introduced ones.

It has been revealed that over the years, I’ve learned that keeping clients isn’t only about delivering good results. It’s also about trust. Clients need to know they can rely on you, especially when something goes wrong. And once that trust is broken, it’s very hard to win back. Alpha Market Flow reports that 72% of repeat buyers say they would permanently abandon a brand after a single trust-breaking incident. That’s why I try to communicate openly, address problems early and never make promises I can’t keep.

Business impact: Focusing on existing clients gives my business more predictable revenue and reduces the constant pressure to find newly introduced projects.

One small habit that has made a significant difference in my marketing work is paying attention to how customers describe their problems. I’ve learned that people rarely use the same language as the companies selling to them.

Industry observers note that I applied this approach with an invoicing software client by studying support tickets, sales calls, live chats, reviews and internal website searches. Customers weren’t asking for an “accounts receivable automation platform.” They wanted to stop chasing late payments, avoid invoice mistakes and save time creating invoices.

I used those insights to build the brand’s narrative. On the client’s own website, I rewrote key pages around the problems customers actually described and added public pricing and customer case studies. Through digital PR campaigns, I made sure that whenever the brand was mentioned on other websites, the surrounding text explained a specific customer problem and how the software solved it. Instead of simply getting mentions, I was consistently telling the same story: This is the tool that helps you get paid on time.

Over six months, the brand earned more than 60 mentions across industry publications, comparison articles and digital PR coverage. Organic traffic increased by 25%, while organic demo requests grew by 44%.

I started using this approach long before AI search became popular, but I believe it’s even more important today. After analyzing 2 million AI citations, Discovered Labs found that content closely matching customers’ questions was more likely to be cited, with stronger alignment associated with roughly 30% more citations. This reinforces something I’ve believed for years: The more consistently you connect your brand to the problems it solves, the easier it becomes for people, and now AI tools, to understand what your business offers.

Business impact: Listening to how customers describe their problems now shapes how I approach every client. When a brand is consistently connected to the problems its customers want solved, it becomes easier to find, easier to trust and easier for both people and AI tools to recommend.

Industry observers note that one habit that has made a real difference in my business is building relationships with journalists before I have something to pitch. I’ve learned that the best media relationships develop gradually, through genuine conversations rather than requests for coverage.

I look for opportunities to connect with journalists at conferences, industry events and in private communities we’re both part of. I also try to understand what matters to them and how I might be helpful, especially when they’re looking for information, sources or expert opinions. I don’t approach every interaction with the expectation of getting something in return.

According to recent reports, even when I’m reading for pleasure or watching television, I often notice journalists whose work interests me. I’ll make a note of their names, look into what they cover and find a natural opportunity to introduce myself. Over time, these small interactions can turn into genuine professional relationships.

Industry observers note that I’ve learned that it’s far better to send a relevant story to 10 or 15 journalists I’ve built relationships with than to blast the same email to 1,500 strangers. Relationships don’t guarantee coverage, but they give you something a mass email can’t: an existing conversation and a better understanding of what each journalist finds interesting.

Sources indicate that these relationships matter to journalists, too. According to CoinFunnel, 53% of journalists consider their relationships with PR professionals important or very important to their success. That reinforces something I’ve learned through experience: Effective PR begins long before you have a story to pitch.

Industry observers note that business impact: Instead of starting from zero every time I have a story to share, I already know which journalists are likely to care about it. That saves time, leads to better conversations and makes it far more likely that my ideas, and my clients’ stories, actually get published.

Industry observers note that if you want to try this yourself, you don’t necessarily have to build these habits one at a time. Many experts recommend starting with a single habit, and that’s good advice in most cases. But because these habits cover very different parts of life and work, I think it’s fine to start a few of them at once.

In a recent development, taking a daily walk won’t get in the way of nurturing relationships with journalists, and working with a trainer won’t stop you from spending more time with existing clients. Pick the ones that fit your life and your business, give them a few months, and pay attention to what changes. Small habits rarely feel key in the moment, but over time, they can shape the kind of business you build.

by Todd Bishop on Nov 19, 2026 at 9:54 amNovember 19, 2026 at 10:09 am.

Anthropic made its Nasdaq debut today in a record $81.3 billion initial public offering, with substantial financial stakes for the Seattle area’s two tech giants.

Sources indicate that for Amazon, the IPO is a paper windfall. The company started putting money into Anthropic in 2023, about $18 billion in all. At the $83 IPO price, its stake was worth about $161 billion. With Anthropic opening at $111.50 a share, that number was closer to $216 billion. The stock has since dropped below $100, which put Amazon’s stake under $200 billion.

Industry observers note that beyond the value of the investment, Anthropic is a major customer for Amazon’s cloud platform. The Claude maker has committed to spend at least $110 billion on Amazon Web Services through 2036.

For Microsoft, it’s more complicated. The Redmond tech giant agreed in late 2025 to invest up to $5 billion but hasn’t disclosed the size of its stake. Microsoft is buying $1 billion of Anthropic stock alongside the IPO, one of seven tech companies buying a combined $26 billion. Anthropic has committed to spend at least $47 billion on Microsoft’s Azure cloud through 2033.

But Microsoft is also pitching its own AI models against Anthropic’s, and it has been working to replace Anthropic’s models with OpenAI’s in some Copilot features, The Information reported this week.

Listing Anthropic’s compute partners on CNBC this morning, co-founder Daniela Amodei named Nvidia, Amazon, Google and Broadcom, but not Microsoft. Whether it was a slip or something more significant, it was an interesting omission.

A historic debut: The offering tops SpaceX’s $75 billion IPO in June, and it makes Anthropic the first standalone AI lab to go public, ahead of OpenAI.

In a recent development, the five-year-old organization was valued at about $1.5 trillion at the $83 IPO price, on a fully diluted basis that counts employee stock and other shares not yet issued. The stock opened at $111.50, valuing Anthropic at about $2 trillion on the same basis. It has since traded as low as about $95.

Speaking before the opening bell, CEO Dario Amodei stated Anthropic will slow the training and release of its AI models for as long as it takes to be confident they’re safe, and that going public only strengthens that resolve.

“We will not bend to either business nor political pressure,” he said.

In an interview with CNBC’s Andrew Ross Sorkin afterward, Amodei called the push and pull between growth and that kind of restraint “one of the central tensions at the heart of the manufacturer.”.

Anthropic is also a public benefit corporation, a structure that legally requires the company to balance shareholders’ interests with the public good.

What’s next: Both Seattle-area giants have hedged their bets. Microsoft owns about 24% of OpenAI, and Amazon put $50 billion into OpenAI earlier this year.

OpenAI, which confidentially filed for its own IPO in June, is still aiming to go public in 2027.

Anthropic’s co-founders and some of its biggest shareholders are barred from selling for up to a year under the IPO’s lock-up rules, and Amazon has said it expects a customary lock-up period.

Amazon will update the value of its Anthropic holdings in its fourth-quarter results, much of it through earnings, which means the paper windfall is likely to boost Amazon’s fourth-quarter profit even though it hasn’t sold a share.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Diesel-electric locomotives have been barreling along America’s wide-open spaces for generations, and the century-old combination of highly efficient diesel engines spinning up generators to power high-torque electric motors has proven tough to beat. Now, Caterpillar is putting that century-old concept to work underground. Meet the CAT R3200 XE LHD.

One of the many hard-working machines moving chunks of Earth under your feet, an LHD (load, haul, and dump) machine is essentially a massive underground wheel loader designed to scoop up blasted rock, haul it through narrow mine tunnels, then dump it into trucks or ore passes. Built low and wide to fit in the tunnels, LHDs are workhorses of underground mining operations – and the newly introduced R3200 XE is CAT’s biggest yet, with a 25 ton payload and electric drive.

Before we get into the machine’s specs (the few that we have, anyway), I want to make sure understand that large-scale mining operations use obscene amounts of fuel, and a swing in site efficiency of just 1-2% can mean a huge difference in the bottom line – and fuel prices were up 27.4% (!) in August alone.

Keep the staggering weight of what that kind of fuel cost can mean to a fleet that buys fuel by the literal truckload as you read the rest of this.

According to recent reports, though not yet officially released by CAT, snippets of the organization’s launch video have been leaking through dealers and trade journals, and they show the massive machine powered by CAT’s newest 18.1 liter Tier 5 C18 diesel generator making 527 hp (~390 kW). That C18 reportedly sends electrons to the same electric drive system used in the company’s already successful 18-ton R2900 XE LHD.

In a recent development, in addition to a bigger generator and heftier payload, CAT says the upcoming R3200 XE LHD offers reduced cycle times versus the R2900 XE with 11% better speed on grade, plus reduced maintenance and repair costs thanks to design refinements for better durability, including redesigned axle. All told, that works out to 28% more tons per hour with 8% better fuel efficiency.

That efficiency is boosted by the same baked-in ADAS tech that’s made the smaller R2900 XE a favorite, and includes the latest version of CAT AutoDig and MineStar, ensuring that the machines are easy for experienced CAT operators to set up for remote, semi-autonomous, and even fully autonomous operation using Command for Underground.

Industry observers note that we’ll post an revision once CAT makes the full rundown of official specs public, which should be sooner rather than later. When that happens, we’ll see exactly how this big burrowing CAT stacks up against the competition from Sandvik, Epiroc, and Komatsu. In the meantime, let us know what you think of CAT’s newest electric drive machine in the comments.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Fed Governor Chris Waller says Americans are starting to treat 3% inflation as normal, and he thinks the central bank may need to “shock people” out of it.
  • It has been revealed that the latest consumer price index also highlighted inflation is heating up more than expected, drifting further away from the Fed’s 2% target.
  • Recent findings suggest that in a CNBC interview on Wednesday, Waller warned that inflation is spreading beyond the areas most affected by higher energy prices or tariffs, including into so-called core services.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Fed Governor Chris Waller says Americans are starting to treat 3% inflation as normal, and he thinks the central bank may need to “shock people” out of it.

It has been revealed that the latest consumer price index also highlighted inflation is heating up more than expected, drifting further away from the Fed’s 2% target. And given that it’s been above that threshold for more than five years, it’s getting harder for consumers and businesses to see higher prices as a temporary blip.

Recent findings suggest that in a CNBC interview on Wednesday, Waller warned that inflation is spreading beyond the areas most affected by higher energy prices or tariffs, including into so-called core services. He recalled talking to someone last week who mentioned his business passed on a 3% price hike to consumers because that’s what he thinks his customers can swallow.

According to recent reports, “And that’s when you start having problems of trying to get inflation down,” Waller explained. “So you might need to, like, shock people to say, ‘Wait a minute, 3% is not the number you should be thinking about going forward.’”.

Once households and businesses expect prices to keep rising 3% a year, they set wages and prices to match, the kind of spiral the Fed worries about after more than five years above its 2% target.

Maintaining consumers’ inflation expectations is a top priority for the Fed. It previously held off on a more hawkish stance, saying expectations were still well anchored. But in Waller’s view, that’s no longer the case.

Industry observers note that “People are starting to think 3% may be the norm. And if you’re a firm, and the consumer’s resilient and seems to be spending, why not pass through three,” Waller warned. “And that’s the kind of psychology we need to start breaking, is that it’s not going to be three, and we have to do something to try to bring it back down. We can’t wait. We can’t do this in, like, the next two years.”.

Because people are starting to become more accepting of higher prices, he thinks the central bank needs to be “a little more aggressive” with rate hikes, including a potential jumbo-size half-point increase at the Fed’s Dec. 8–9 meetings.

It has been revealed that A half-point move would lift the Fed’s benchmark rate to a range of 4.25% to 4.5%, from 3.75% to 4% now. The Fed raised rates in September for the first time in more than three years, then held steady in October.

According to recent reports, wall Street isn’t there yet. Futures are fully pricing in a quarter-point hike in December, according to CME Group’s FedWatch tool. Waller said a quarter-point could do the job if the Fed clearly signaled another hike in January. But Fed Chair Kevin Warsh has been against that kind of forward guidance on the grounds that it ties policymakers’ hands.

The problem has been complicated by the fact that the effects of President Donald Trump’s tariffs have been dragged out instead of hitting all at once, as negotiations and legal challenges kept the levies on again and off again. Meanwhile, businesses didn’t pass on the full cost of tariffs at once but spread it out.

Industry observers note that at the same time, the Iran war doesn’t seem to be winding down anytime soon as Trump has shot down further talks. Although oil prices have come down from highs, they are still volatile and spike whenever fighting in the Persian Gulf heats up again. The cumulative effect is weighing on attitudes.

Minutes from the Fed’s October meeting, released the same day as Waller’s interview, back up his worry: Fed staff flagged the risk that longer-run inflation expectations could have become unanchored after five years of elevated inflation.

On Friday, Fed Governor Lisa Cook echoed Waller’s concerns about consumer psychology as she explained her dissenting vote to hike rates at the last meeting.

“My vote reflected the urgency I feel to tackle inflation,” which “has been above target for more than ‌five and ⁠a half years, and every additional day poses greater risk that price- and wage-setters will adjust their inflation expectations upward,” she noted, according to the text of a speech to be presented at a conference in Chile.

Recent findings suggest that still, other policymakers signaled more caution. Fresh York Fed President John Williams noted on Tuesday that there’s no need for “dramatic action,” arguing that the more gradual approach in recent months is working well.

Industry observers note that he added that the economy remains resilient and the labor market is solid, even as he acknowledged that inflation isn’t moving in the right direction. But that resilience is also what’s allowing businesses to pass on bigger price hikes.

It has been revealed that as a result, one big hike may not be the end of it. Waller remarked the Fed needs to reverse the three rate cuts it made in 2025, and may have to go further.

“If the policy rate last summer in 2025 wasn’t bringing inflation down, getting back to that isn’t going to bring it down,” he told CNBC. “So we may have to go above … three hikes plus maybe some more to get it to start actually coming back down.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

In a recent development, I run a global business called Brand of a Leader, which supports founders and executives in more than 12 countries by helping them build their visibility. When I first released my business six years ago, all I had was a LinkedIn profile — no website and, naturally, no digital footprint of any kind yet.

And so our first few clients came through my network. By being active on LinkedIn and consistently sharing my perspective, I would stay top of mind with people who already knew me. When they needed support, or when someone in their own network did, I was the one who came to mind and was hired or recommended.

Sources indicate that today, I continue to use LinkedIn actively to generate clients, develop relationships and stay connected with my network. I’ve been on the platform for over 20 years, and throughout the years, I’ve heard people constantly complain about one thing: the algorithm. I always chuckle because the discourse is consistently the same, yet it’s presented as something new. Through all of my work and my extensive work supporting founders across the globe with their LinkedIn, I’ve seen how much people overindex on what to post, when to post and how to post, while overlooking something else that is likely even more important!

Here are the three mistakes I see founders make all the time. And I promise that if you fix those, you will see better results from this platform.

It has been revealed that obsession over what, when and how to post is real. Short posts or long posts? Daily or weekly? With a photo? Video? No media? What should I even write about? Those are undoubtedly important questions, yet there’s another one: What happens when someone reads your post, does become interested in learning more about you and then clicks on your profile?

Industry observers note that my experience highlights me that most founders don’t pay much attention to what’s actually on their profile. I know this because I constantly audit LinkedIn pages as part of the service that we provide at Brand of a Leader.

Sources indicate that too often, when I visit a LinkedIn profile, I find a bland banner or none whatsoever, and a short “About” section written in the third person. Whatever interest the person’s post may have piqued is swiftly lost when visiting their uninspiring profile.

Personally, I treat my profile as a landing page. And we do the same for our clients. For entrepreneurs, myself included, a well-designed LinkedIn page can be a practical alternative to a personal website when used thoughtfully.

Visit your profile, looking at it through the eyes of a potential client, and see what impression it would leave on them after spending a minute or two scrolling through it.

According to recent reports, one of the things we consistently convince our clients not to do is include calls to action in their posts. Salesy or overly promotional messages on founders’ profiles don’t make a great impression.

Industry observers note that as a reader, I find that repeated prompts to book a call can make otherwise thoughtful writing feel overly promotional. I prefer to keep my content, and my clients’ content, conversational, expertise-building or humanizing. Yet, I do understand the importance of giving interested readers a clearly visible way to take the next step.

It has been revealed that instead of salesy calls to action in posts, I leverage the custom call-to-action button included with LinkedIn Premium Business. You can have it say anything that’s most relevant to you and your goals (for example, “Visit my website” or “Book a call”). This link will appear in your profile, just under your name and above the post that you write. That feels more elegant to me.

In a recent development, one of the biggest mistakes I see founders make is treating LinkedIn as a broadcasting platform and not a social media platform. This is not only the quickest way to reduce the overall engagement of your content on LinkedIn, but it’s also not great for your positioning overall. When you only post and never engage, it positions you as a taker, not a giver, and also discourages people from further engaging with you.

It has been revealed that at a minimum, you need to reply to people who took the time to comment on your posts. No, not only a “like” — an actual thoughtful reply. They have taken time to respond to something you shared. Read their contribution and respond to the substance of it.

Sources indicate that and then ideally, extend that attention to other people’s content. Comment to share a relevant experience or ask a thoughtful question. If someone describes a challenge you have faced, explain what you learned. But don’t use AI. Generic, bland comments negatively impact your brand equity. Take 30 minutes to leave some authentic comments a couple of times weekly, and that consistency will compound over time.

Before publishing your next post, think about what interested readers will see on your profile if they click on it. Give them enough context to understand your expertise, an easy way to contact you and your attention when they engage in conversation with you.

Industry observers note that before you hit publish again, take a look at LinkedIn’s new Small Business Playbook for practical ways to build your brand, grow your network and find customers. You can also explore LinkedIn’s tools for small businesses to make sure your profile is ready when interested readers click through.

  • In 2010, the revolution began: 10,000 BTC was used to buy two pizzas, one of the first uses of the digital asset in exchange for a commodity.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On this day, 17 years ago, Satoshi Nakamoto opened an account on BitcoinTalk, the place that would become the home of early Bitcoin enthusiasts and then turn into a public forum for crypto in general, until social media platforms took over the internet.

Sources indicate that the network itself was barely 1 year old, and its future raised more questions than answers. Satoshi Nakamoto welcomed users on the forum and invited any questions people had regarding the cryptocurrency.

In 2010, the revolution began: 10,000 BTC was used to buy two pizzas, one of the first uses of the digital asset in exchange for a commodity. In May, Laszlo Hanyecz probably had the most expensive pizza dinner in history, considering how much BTC rallied after that. By December, Satoshi made their final BitcoinTalk post and announced their farewell.

The 2011-2014 period turned out to be the foundation for the network as a whole. Bitcoin became an open-source project maintained by others. The first halving happened in November 2012 and reduced the block issuance from 50 to 25 BTC per block.

The first-ever exchange implosion, Mt.Gox in 2014, raised serious questions about the security and stability of centralized exchanges, an issue we haven't solved 17 years later.

Sources indicate that 2017-2021 were the years when the industry truly blossomed. We had our first bull run on Bitcoin, which pushed the price above expected levels, to almost $20,000 in December 2017, along with the first altcoin bull run and the birth of upcoming technologies like smart contracts, NFTs and many more. The next cycle took Bitcoin to around $69,000 in November 2021.

It has been revealed that however, with the growth of the industry, multiple conflicts arose around safety, integrity and usage. The first country in the world to adopt Bitcoin was El Salvador, which implemented the digital currency as a true means of payment, in addition to accumulating it in its treasury.

Sources indicate that 2022 was the pivotal year, marked by the FTX and Terra crashes that changed how investors treat markets in general. FTX wasn't just an exchange: it was the backbone of the cryptocurrency market in those years. It aimed to rival Binance and become the bridge between institutional investors and crypto.

However, poor risk management, complications with fund allocation and many other factors caused an implosion that ended the bull run.

In 2024, Wall Street arrived in crypto with ETFs, ETPs, perpetual futures and a regulatory framework. The digital assets industry became a part of a larger market. Whether that is good or bad is a question to consider, but one thing is clear: Bitcoin has come a very long way since 2010 and is evolving to this day.

The next step is the arrival of AI and rising cybersecurity risks, which go toe-to-toe with the quantum danger. How the first cryptocurrency handles them is a question that directly affects its future.

#18758. Yield-Bearing eZAR Blurs the Line Between Stablecoin and Investment Product

Yield-Bearing eZAR Blurs the Line Between Stablecoin and Investment Product

📅 03 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1362 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nulltx

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • eZAR opened its rand-pegged token to the public on November 2 with R303 million in circulation.
  • Most stablecoin introduces promise a token that never moves.
  • Industry observers note that according to launch reports, eZAR is now open to the public and to new institutional partners after almost a year of pilot operations.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

eZAR opened its rand-pegged token to the public on November 2 with R303 million in circulation. Its reserve yield is the feature that puts the stablecoin label to the test.

Most stablecoin introduces promise a token that never moves. eZAR's disclosures say its holders can make money or lose it. The rand-pegged token went live to the public on November 2, and its fine print reads more like an investment product than a payments coin.

Industry observers note that according to launch reports, eZAR is now open to the public and to new institutional partners after almost a year of pilot operations. The company notes R303 million worth of tokens had been issued and were in circulation as of October 30.

The project is a partnership between eZAR Ltd, asset manager Ninety One and AVBOB Financial Services, with AVBOB acting as lead institution and liquidity partner. CEO Sean Emery stated the team put "getting it right" ahead of "getting it significant" during the pilot. The message now is that eZAR is ready to scale.

Recent findings suggest that the model also departs from the typical single-issuer coin. Neobanks, retailers, insurers and payment firms can plug the token into their own branded wallets and share in the economics. Transfers between participating wallets settle within seconds at any hour and, according to the tech giant, cost nothing.

It has been revealed that the reserves backing eZAR are invested through a money market strategy run by Ninety One, mainly in the Ninety One Money Market Fund. Returns are distributed daily to partners after partnership fees, and each partner then decides on what terms its own customers receive a share.

Ninety One's head of digital assets, Adam Duxbury, described it as newly introduced rails under an old discipline. His firm has run money market strategies for 25 years, he mentioned, and South Africa should build its own digital rand rather than import a dollar coin.

The framing is clever, since it presents the yield as a feature of "digital cash that can grow." Yet that same feature makes the classification question hard to avoid.

According to recent reports, the risk language is the most revealing part of the launch. eZAR describes itself as a crypto asset issued by the eZAR En Commandite Partnership. It states that the token is not legal tender, not a bank deposit and not a banking product, and that it carries no guarantee.

The details that follow set it further apart. The R1 redemption value depends on available liquidity. Money market returns can be positive or negative, so capital is at risk. Holders also own no units in the underlying fund and have no direct claim on it.

"Capital at risk" rarely appears in stablecoin terms. A payments token is meant to hold its value and let users redeem at par, yet eZAR's own documents hedge on both counts. Back in March, a market survey from Blockhouse had already noted that eZAR doesn't qualify as a stablecoin under most regulations. The live launch now tests that observation against a real product.

In the major rulebooks, the yield is the sticking point. The US GENIUS Act bars permitted payment stablecoin issuers from paying holders any form of interest or yield solely for holding, using or retaining the token. The EU's MiCA framework takes a similar line on interest. The logic is that a payment token paying a return starts to function like an unregulated deposit.

Sources indicate that the OCC issued its final GENIUS Act rules on October 21, and they confirmed that ban for covered issuers. The contested ground lies elsewhere, in who sits between the issuer and the holder. Earlier OCC proposals set a rebuttable presumption against yield arrangements run through affiliates and related third parties, whereas the statute itself names only issuers.

In a recent development, eZAR's design lands squarely in that gray zone. Returns flow to partners, and the partners decide how customers share in them. Whether that amounts to an issuer paying yield or a partner passing on profit is precisely the kind of question US regulators are now wrestling with, and it would be a difficult one to argue before the OCC.

eZAR doesn't operate under the US or EU regimes, so none of those rules apply to it directly. eZAR Ltd is described as an authorised financial services provider responsible for the main technology and services behind the partnership. That technology also draws on the South African Reserve Bank's Project Khokha 2, where eZAR's parent tech giant, Block Markets Africa, was a technical contributor.

It has been revealed that this background signals a serious, institution-backed build rather than a speculative launch. Even so, the rand stablecoin field is getting crowded. ZARU launched earlier this year as an institutional-grade rand coin, and a pattern is emerging of different models competing for the same local payments niche.

Recent findings suggest that the bigger question is whether South Africa will define stablecoins narrowly, as the US and EU do, or leave room for hybrid products like this one. Because the network is permissioned, the reported circulation figure also rests on company disclosure rather than a public ledger, which makes the regulatory and disclosure framework matter even more.

According to recent reports, for everyday consumers, the appeal is easy to see. A rand token that moves in seconds, costs nothing to send and might earn a daily return makes an attractive pitch. For partners, shared infrastructure with a revenue share offers a way into digital payments without building a coin from scratch.

In a recent development, the trade-off sits in the disclaimers. A holder who treats eZAR like a bank balance could be caught off guard by liquidity-dependent redemption, or by a money market return that dips below zero. That gap between how the product feels and how it is legally defined is where regulators tend to step in.

eZAR is best understood as a hybrid: a payments token with an investment return attached. It may well succeed on those terms. Still, as more jurisdictions tighten the stablecoin definition around no-yield, par-redemption tokens, products like this will increasingly be judged on what they are rather than what they are called. How South African regulators treat eZAR in the coming months will show which way that debate is heading.

Uncommon Thinkers: Andrew Redd’s audacious blueprint to turn ocean volcanoes into power plants

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1234 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Geekwire

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 19, 2026 at 10:07 amNovember 19, 2026 at 4:42 pm.
  • Editor’s note: This series profiles five Seattle-area “Uncommon Thinkers,” who will be recognized Dec.
  • Andrew Redd‘s career path creates a tidy narrative: grow up in Seattle steeped in aviation and maritime culture, study mechanical engineering and aerospace, work at SpaceX, then launch an offshore geothermal energy startup.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 19, 2026 at 10:07 amNovember 19, 2026 at 4:42 pm.

Editor’s note: This series profiles five Seattle-area “Uncommon Thinkers,” who will be recognized Dec. 10 at the GeekWire Gala in partnership with Greater Seattle Partners.

Andrew Redd‘s career path creates a tidy narrative: grow up in Seattle steeped in aviation and maritime culture, study mechanical engineering and aerospace, work at SpaceX, then launch an offshore geothermal energy startup.

The dots connect, but the picture they form is anything but ordinary: bold in vision, fast in execution and enormous in potential.

Redd has next-level ambition, and he’s directing it at solving one of the world’s biggest and most urgent problems — adding renewable, massively scalable energy that can outcompete fossil fuels and reach the grid promptly enough to make a difference in the race against climate change.

Recent findings suggest that underwater geothermal energy has never been tapped in a significant way, but to Redd, the idea was irresistible. “It checks all of the boxes for our perfect future energy source,” he said.

He founded Endurance Energy on the north shore of Seattle’s Lake Union in January 2025, and this September the team oversaw its fifth deep-sea deployment. At a site 300 miles off the Oregon coast, its prototype system generated more electricity than it consumed. The startup has raised $63 million from investors and has roughly three dozen employees.

Industry observers note that nate Bek, a principal at Ascend, praised Redd’s ability to attract “brilliant” talent in pursuit of his goal. The Seattle venture firm is one of the startup’s early backers.

Sources indicate that “I’ve been deeply inspired by what [Redd]’s building at Endurance and haven’t shut up about it since the day we met,” Bek noted. “He somehow makes powering the world from the bottom of the ocean feel inevitable, all while remaining remarkably measured and transparent about the progress.”.

According to recent reports, for Redd, studying engineering and aerospace in college was so clear-cut that it wasn’t a choice at all. Growing up around Boeing, seaplanes, the Museum of Flight and the Pacific Northwest’s rich maritime industry naturally pointed him toward those sectors. He wanted a degree as expansive as his influences.

Recent findings suggest that “I didn’t really want to have to choose whether it was going to be boats or space travel or airplanes,” he stated. “I just wanted to be able to do anything — keep the world as wide open as possible.”.

After graduating from Princeton University, Redd worked at Neuralink, an Elon Musk company developing technology that lets the brain communicate directly with computers. A year later, in 2021, he moved to Musk’s rocket company, SpaceX.

That was another no-duh decision, as Redd viewed it.

“I saw SpaceX as really the place to be, where early-career people are given the most amount of resources and responsibility, and that felt like the fastest way to learn and the most engaging possible scenario to be in,” Redd remarked. “I wanted to be tossed into something that was a little bit crazy.”.

According to recent reports, redd joined as SpaceX was starting to build its first orbital Starship rockets. The program brought together passionate young people and experienced SpaceX engineers who served as mentors. Wild ideas were entertained and explored. Everyone was committed to the mission. It was just the experience Redd wanted, and he planned to stick around for seven to 10 years.

Then artificial intelligence started booming.

In 2024, the build-out of sprawling, energy-hungry data centers for AI was accelerating with no end in sight. At the same time, efforts to electrify transportation, heating and cooling were driving up demand for power. Redd saw these trends sparking a surge in new natural gas generation, locking in decades of carbon emissions.

He wanted to find a better way. He went into engineering mode, focusing on all the essential criteria for an energy source: it had to be clean, not dependent on intermittent sun or wind, capable of producing massive amounts of energy, readily deployable, subject to fewer regulatory hurdles than something like nuclear, economically competitive, and scalable.

According to recent reports, redd recognized the tremendous heat contained under Earth’s surface as a terrific source for renewable energy and realized that most of the world’s active volcanoes are offshore. The unknown was whether the rocky ocean floor would be suitable for geothermal wells, so he did some research and found publications from geology experts who said the conditions would be “perfect.”.

“You can tell,” he said, “when there’s a moment in time that you need to go and reach out and grab something, and that was really my impression — if I didn’t start this now, this would never come into existence, or wouldn’t come into existence soon enough to make a meaningful impact.”.

It has been revealed that in launching Endurance, Redd was intentional about the culture he wanted to create. He was aiming for a multidisciplinary group of mission-driven employees eager to collaborate and learn from each other: top talent that would attract more of the same and make Endurance a place people were excited to work.

“The hardest part of an early-stage startup is recruiting,” Redd remarked, “especially if you’re a first-time founder.”.

The startup employs about a dozen SpaceX alumni, plus employees from the fusion company Helion Energy and the aerospace venture Blue Origin.

It has been revealed that A strong team is key to Endurance’s success. That’s because, enthusiasm and passion aside, the startup faces steep engineering and economic challenges. The technology must withstand high pressure, corrosive conditions and mineral scaling inside devices, and seafloor machinery could be costly to repair. The systems will need expensive subsea cables to carry power to shore over potentially long distances. It’s a heavy lift.

While the September sea trial didn’t go perfectly, Redd is happy with the results. The organization landed its 3-ton power plant on the seafloor near a natural vent and produced net energy from it — albeit for only 8.7 seconds. Technical difficulties and a power-cable failure cut the dive short.

Team members successfully operated the system remotely from Seattle through a fiber-optic network running along the seabed. Redd mentioned he’s grateful for access to the network, which is part of the National Science Foundation’s Regional Cabled Array and operated by the University of Washington.

Endurance engineers also drilled what they called the world’s first subsea geothermal well at a site about 5,000 feet below the ocean’s surface. The 2-inch-wide, 52-foot-deep well delivered hydrothermal fluid, but the flow was too restricted to run the power plant, sending the team to the natural vent.

Redd remarked there’s a lot of work ahead, but the team “made huge strides” in learning and in reducing the project’s risks.

The manufacturer now is developing Leopard, its 2-megawatt generator. After testing the technology at the research site off the Oregon coast, Endurance aims to deliver power from a Leopard system in Tonga next year as its first commercial project. Subsea geothermal energy could ultimately reduce the island nation’s reliance on imported diesel and put the startup one step closer to its objective of generating terawatts of planet-friendly energy.

In a recent development, “This was always the end goal,” Redd remarked. “Create something that is highly meaningful for the world.”.

Editor’s Note: Nate Bek of Ascend is a former GeekWire reporter.

Industry News: Polestar unveils Formula 2030 concept, previewing the next Polestar 2

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1309 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Polestar has now fully unveiled the Formula 2030 concept, a low four-door electric sports car that previews the design of the next-generation Polestar 2 coming in 2027 and the Polestar 7 compact SUV.
  • The concept sits just 1,350 mm (53 inches) tall, which is lower than the Polestar 5 grand tourer, and it brings physical buttons back into the Swedish brand’s interior.
  • According to recent reports, we reported in September that Polestar confirmed the Formula 2030 concept after showing it privately to investors and retailers in Gothenburg.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Polestar has now fully unveiled the Formula 2030 concept, a low four-door electric sports car that previews the design of the next-generation Polestar 2 coming in 2027 and the Polestar 7 compact SUV.

The concept sits just 1,350 mm (53 inches) tall, which is lower than the Polestar 5 grand tourer, and it brings physical buttons back into the Swedish brand’s interior.

According to recent reports, we reported in September that Polestar confirmed the Formula 2030 concept after showing it privately to investors and retailers in Gothenburg. Now we get the full set of pictures and the details.

It’s the first show car built under head of design Philipp Römers, who joined from Audi in 2024.

Polestar calls the Formula 2030 a “compact practical four-door sports car” that “sits within its own segment.” It’s 4,680 mm (184.3 inches) long and 2,021 mm (79.6 inches) wide, on a 2,780 mm (109.4-inch) wheelbase.

Sources indicate that for context, that’s about 3 inches longer than today’s Polestar 2 and roughly 5 inches lower. It’s also a bit shorter than a Tesla Model 3 and sits 3.5 inches closer to the ground. Polestar states the concept lands “somewhere between” the upcoming Polestar 2 and Polestar 7 in size.

The proportions are classic sports car: long hood, short overhangs, the cabin pushed back over big rear haunches, and 22-inch center-lock wheels. There are gold Brembo calipers behind those wheels and Öhlins dampers on display in the trunk.

According to recent reports, up front, Polestar kept its “Dual Blade” headlights, now set into an aero wing over a shark nose and a deep splitter. The automaker says this is the face of the next-generation Polestar 2 planned for 2027.

There’s a single vertical windshield wiper, like on a race car, and a LiDAR unit that hides under an aerodynamic shroud and only reveals itself when the car is driving autonomously.

The rear is where things change the most. Polestar dropped the full-width light bar, which is on just about every EV these days, for what it calls “Single Blade” rear lights. It indicates they are being introduced here “ahead of series production.”.

Römers described the concept as a “bold evolution” of the brand’s existing design:.

“It is a physical embodiment of how we apply Polestar’s core values of design, performance and sustainability to the next production cars.”.

The rear doors are hinged at the back and there’s no B-pillar, so the whole side opens up to four individual seats.

The interior is built around the driver. A curved 20-inch display, which Polestar calls the “HyperDIM,” is mounted directly on the steering column, and a 12.2-inch center screen sits in the center tunnel.

Recent findings suggest that but the bigger news is below that screen. Polestar added a panel of eight physical controls for the most-used functions, and owners could swap between types of controls, like rocker switches or rotary knobs, and program what each one does.

Polestar says it is “committing to rebalance the mix of physical and digital.” Juan Pablo Bernal, the firm’s head of interior design, put it plainly:.

In a recent development, “As a performance brand, we see a renewed focus on the driver, and so we re-balance the digital and physical. We introduce physical buttons and controls.”.

That’s a big change for a brand whose recent cars run almost everything through the center touchscreen.

Industry observers note that the cabin also physically changes with the drive mode. There are three of them: Performance, Normal, and Autonomous. In Performance, the center screen drops flush into the console and the steering wheel and its display pull closer to the driver. In Autonomous, the wheel and the seat move away from each other.

In a recent development, the four seats use inflatable bolsters that shape themselves to each occupant, and the seat backs are made of a flax-based composite instead of virgin plastic. Google Gemini is built in, like in Polestar’s production cars.

The cargo area is the strangest part of the car. The rear opens as a clamshell, and the trunk floor is transparent, with custom Polestar bags strapped down underneath it with gold straps.

Up front, the frunk holds two race helmets and a fire extinguisher, framed by a gold strut brace.

In a recent development, now for what’s missing. Polestar didn’t release a single powertrain spec. No battery size, no range, no power output, and no price. This is a design study, and Polestar isn’t saying it will build it.

What it does say is that “various design attributes” from the concept will show up on the next Polestar 2 in 2027 and the Polestar 7 in 2028. Those are two of the four new models Polestar prepares to launch in three years, and the 7 is going to be built in Europe.

Europe is where this matters, since Polestar is shut out of the US under the federal connected-vehicle rule. The concept made its debut during the media drive of the Polestar 4 SUV.

Polestar always impresses me with its design, and this is no exception with this fresh head of design.

The proportions are sharp. Long hood, cabin pushed back, big haunches, and a roofline lower than the Polestar 5’s on a car with four doors and four real seats. If the next Polestar 2 keeps even half of this stance, it’s going to be the best-looking car in its segment.

Recent findings suggest that I have loved Polestar from the day they rolled out. Every car they design is a work of art and I love their commitment to transparency and sustainablitity. The 2023 Polestar 2 is still one of my favorite cars I've ever owned. I've driven the 3 and the 4 and both were fantastic. The fit and finish, ride and build quality, and NVH were all excellent. The upgraded 3 was probably going to be my next car in 2027 until they were forced to withdraw from the US. I think their future with the new 2 and 7 are bright and I'm still hoping (though I'm not holding my breath) that they will return to the US at some point. If the 5 was available here, I'd buy it today.

In a recent development, I don’t know about the trunk of this thing. Polestar itself calls the rear “UFO-esque,” and between the wraparound glass, the clamshell and the see-through floor, it’s a lot. But everything else on this car is pretty sharp.

Polestar is putting physical controls back in its cars and saying so in plain words. The way they talk about it makes it sound like you can expect that of upcoming production vehicles.

Now the usual caveat. A concept car doesn’t fix a balance sheet. Polestar lost $842 million in the first half of this year on a negative gross margin. Design has never been Polestar’s problem. Building these cars and selling them at a profit is.

How to Harness the Power of Human Interaction to Win Customers Over This Holiday Season

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.
  • As the fourth quarter rolls around, entrepreneurs everywhere hope to close out a productive year.
  • AI can accomplish a lot, but it still falls short when it comes to the magic of personal touch.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

As the fourth quarter rolls around, entrepreneurs everywhere hope to close out a productive year. This season sparks a flurry of activity for businesses, especially those eager to capitalize on fall and holiday shoppers. No matter your industry, the holiday season is the ideal moment to highlight the power of genuine human connection.

AI can accomplish a lot, but it still falls short when it comes to the magic of personal touch. It’s easy to see how positive human interaction can boost your business during the holidays, but these same tactics belong in your everyday playbook. Let’s explore a few simple ways the human touch can spark joy that goes far beyond your bottom line.

Recent findings suggest that I have to confess, there are moments when I catch myself sounding like someone from an older generation. Every day, I remind my staff to return client calls promptly and reply to emails without delay. Though I’m only in my late 40s, I notice a shift in my younger colleagues. Like a fading sense of urgency and a dwindling desire for personal interaction.

Perhaps it’s a wish to sidestep conflict or uncomfortable conversations. I understand that urge. Still, I’ve learned that the fastest way to resolve a tough client situation is through genuine human touch. I’m not referring to physical touch, but honest, direct communication delivered with empathy and understanding. On the other hand, leading with human touch from the start can forge deeper bonds and lasting appreciation with customers.

Recent findings suggest that you’ve probably heard the saying, “size matters.” While that might hold true in some cases, my own transcription organization is small compared to many others. Yet, the personal touch we practice and that I encourage my team to deliver works just as well for medium and large businesses alike.

Most of our first interactions with clients begin on our website, where a potential customer fills out our contact form. That’s our first chance to connect personally, to reach out and add a human touch. Here’s an example of how a team member might respond to a website inquiry.

Industry observers note that “Thanks for reaching out, Jane. We’d love to assist you with your court hearing transcripts. When do you need them completed and sent back?”.

It has been revealed that let’s unpack our initial email. First, we always address the person by name. If they include a title, we use it, whether it’s Dr. Smith or Detective Jones. Second, we acknowledge their inquiry as rapidly as possible, ideally within 15 minutes. Finally, we ask for permission to connect more personally. A phone conversation with a potential customer lets us highlight our services and, even more importantly, our commitment to detail.

Sources indicate that most people appreciate the chance to talk by phone. For those who prefer email, there are still plenty of ways to add a personal touch throughout the exchange. Whether we’re on the phone or typing an email, we make it a point to ask open-ended questions that encourage the other person to share more. This is a classic strategy sales trainers recommend everywhere.

The holiday season offers your team even more chances to make a lasting impression through personal interaction. We keep it simple with a cheerful “Happy Holidays,” but if a client mentions a specific celebration, i.e., Thanksgiving, Christmas, Hanukkah or Kwanzaa, then we ask how they are enjoying their favorite season.

In a recent development, finally, our team always aims to have the last word. When a customer pays an invoice, we don’t just send an automated “Thank you for your payment.” Instead, we follow up with a personal email to our main contact, giving us one more opportunity to add a genuine human touch.

In a recent development, what exactly will your business or tech giant gain through human touch? Trust. Customers, more specifically, individuals, want to know they can trust you to deliver a service or product.

Industry observers note that it’s true that most companies can build some trust without much human interaction. If you add a personal touch, it speeds up the process and makes it feel more genuine. Too often, human interaction only happens when something goes wrong. While it’s smart to use a personal approach to solve problems, starting every client relationship with a human touch lays a strong foundation for when challenges pop up later.

Sources indicate that people with a personal relationship with an employee or tech giant respond to challenges very differently than those without one. That’s simply human nature.

Personally, I get frustrated when I can’t reach a real person with a question or concern. Endless phone trees and chatbots that never connect you to a human leave me feeling anything but trust. Here are a few ways to boost human interaction:.

Sources indicate that if Emily Post, the famed etiquette expert of the early 20th century, were still with us, I’m sure she’d have plenty to say about the power of handwritten notes. Even though I haven’t found a definitive study on their impact, my own experience tells me that few things leave a stronger impression than a personally written letter or note.

I think the magic of a handwritten note starts with the effort it takes. Printing a form letter or invoice is easy, but writing a note by hand and addressing the envelope takes real time and care. Even jotting a quick sentence or two at the bottom of a printed letter can make a lasting impression.

Industry observers note that last month, I received a statement from the tech giant that acquired the self-storage facility I use. Because of a glitch when switching back-end systems, I didn’t receive an invoice for a couple of months, which resulted in the new owner placing their lock on my unit. A quick phone call resolved the situation and also gave the new company a chance to introduce themselves.

The next week, I received an invoice with a handwritten note from the owner. He apologized for the mistake, thanked me for my business and invited me to reach out directly with any questions or concerns. Even with a rate increase, his personal effort left a positive impression.

It has been revealed that the holiday season in the fourth quarter gives businesses a golden chance to thank both new and loyal customers for their support. Gift baskets, charitable donations in their name, party invites or even a simple greeting card (ideally signed by a real person) are all thoughtful ways to share holiday cheer.

But why limit these gestures to just the holidays? Why not carry these strategies through all 12 months of the year?

Sources indicate that many entrepreneurs and business owners use the holidays as a chance for personal, even face-to-face, connections. Each holiday season, I spend a few weeks personally delivering homemade gourmet treats to clients across Colorado. Without an outside sales team, these personal holiday visits have become a winning strategy for us. Plus, they love and eagerly anticipate the gourmet homemade goodies I deliver.

Recent findings suggest that this also reminds me that personal visits shouldn’t happen only once a year. In fact, they should be a regular occurrence. Personal interaction, especially when it comes from the owner, is a powerful strategy that deserves a permanent spot on the calendar.

Industry observers note that don’t forget to reach out to customers you haven’t connected with in a while. The holidays are a perfect time to show your appreciation, but make it a goal to check in with every customer at least once a quarter.

Here’s a reminder not to neglect your internal staff: Employees and team members need and deserve recognition. Schedule a lunch, dinner or get-together to show appreciation and thank everyone for making your clients and customers feel valued.

It has been revealed that as the fourth quarter rolls around, entrepreneurs everywhere hope to close out a productive year. This season sparks a flurry of activity for businesses, especially those eager to capitalize on fall and holiday shoppers. No matter your industry, the holiday season is the ideal moment to highlight the power of genuine human connection.

AI can accomplish a lot, but it still falls short when it comes to the magic of personal touch. It’s easy to see how positive human interaction can boost your business during the holidays, but these same tactics belong in your everyday playbook. Let’s explore a few simple ways the human touch can spark joy that goes far beyond your bottom line.

It has been revealed that I have to confess, there are moments when I catch myself sounding like someone from an older generation. Every day, I remind my staff to return client calls promptly and reply to emails without delay. Though I’m only in my late 40s, I notice a shift in my younger colleagues. Like a fading sense of urgency and a dwindling desire for personal interaction.
