It’s that time again – Honda needs to roll out an electric Super Cub

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (875 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Every few years, I apparently feel compelled to remind Honda that it is sitting on what could be one of the easiest home runs in the electric motorcycle industry: just make an electric Super Cub already.
  • I’m not talking about an electric scooter vaguely inspired by the Super Cub.
  • Sources indicate that the Honda Super Cub is arguably the most successful motor vehicle ever created, with well over 100 million produced since its introduction in 1958.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Every few years, I apparently feel compelled to remind Honda that it is sitting on what could be one of the easiest home runs in the electric motorcycle industry: just make an electric Super Cub already.

I’m not talking about an electric scooter vaguely inspired by the Super Cub. Not another futuristic concept with swoopy bodywork and a name that looks like a Wi-Fi password. I mean an actual honest-to-goodness Honda Super Cub, except electric.

The formula is already sitting right there.

Sources indicate that the Honda Super Cub is arguably the most successful motor vehicle ever created, with well over 100 million produced since its introduction in 1958. It’s still in continuous production today.

Recent findings suggest that and a huge part of that success comes down to how approachable the thing is. It isn’t supposed to be intimidating, excessively powerful, or particularly complicated. It’s simple, practical transportation wrapped in one of the most recognizable two-wheeler designs ever created.

In other words, it’s practically begging to become electric.

It has been revealed that the beauty of the bike is how simple and timeless it is, with the appearance barely changing in nearly 7 decades. And with the design freedom that electric drivetrains provide, upgrading the cute little bike to an electric future would be a walk in the park for Honda’s engineers.

An in-wheel motor would be a simple, cheap solution that frees up even more space in the body for batteries.

According to recent reports, and Honda wouldn’t need some enormous battery capable of highway touring. Give an electric Super Cub enough battery for perhaps 50-60 miles (80-95 km) of real-world urban riding, a motor capable of roughly 50-60 mph (80-95 km/h), and simple Level 1 charging from a normal wall outlet. As a city runabout or a beachside cruiser, those middle-of-the-road specs would be perfect.

Even better, make the battery removable. Honda already has its Mobile Power Pack e: swappable battery system used in various electric two-wheelers, and an electric Super Cub would be an incredible platform to expand it.

The resulting bike could hit an unusually sweet spot.

It has been revealed that there are millions of people riding electric bicycles today who will eventually want something faster, but don’t necessarily want a 500-pound (220 kg) electric motorcycle capable of hitting 120 mph (200 km/h). An electric Super Cub would be a natural next step: light, unintimidating, easy to ride, cheap to operate, and fast enough to actually function as a real urban vehicle.

It would also be one of the rare electric motorcycles that could appeal to people who aren’t necessarily looking for an “electric motorcycle.” An electric version is in such high demand that companies specialize in retrofit kits to convert classic Cubs into EVs.

The Super Cub already has decades of cultural cachet. It’s cute. It’s useful. It’s nostalgic without feeling ancient. It’s the kind of motorcycle that can appeal equally to a lifelong rider and someone who has never considered owning a motorcycle before.

And perhaps most importantly, Honda could actually sell the thing globally. The same basic electric Super Cub could work in dense European cities, throughout Asia, and in American cities and suburbs. It doesn’t need to win spec-sheet battles. It just needs to be affordable, reliable, and unmistakably a Super Cub.

My mum's old Honda-50 (the original cub, early 70's) had a tank that held less than a gallon of petrol. Range was realistically about 50 miles, but no-one even thought about that, it never ran out.

She traded for a honda-90, then a bunch of other stuff, I miss that 90, even now.

But the point is that range is not the matter, very few trips on these are more than 10 - 15 miles, say 30km round-trip.

But the real range, on a battery vehicle, is only about 2/3 of the claim,.

so if the claim is 80, it'll maybe do 55?

Thats enough, if it has the zip to handle traffic, and cruise at 45 - 50mph.

It has been revealed that honda has already shown that it understands the importance of electrifying small two-wheelers. It’s even made a token gesture with a Cub-like e-scooter in China. But there’s a difference between making another electric scooter and electrifying perhaps the most famous small motorcycle ever made.

So here I am once again, Honda.

According to recent reports, you’ve got the name. You’ve got the design. You’ve got the batteries. You’ve got the manufacturing scale.

Just put all the pieces together and give us the electric Super Cub already. The world is waiting, and will thank you.

It has been revealed that NEAR Protocol (NEAR) fell 11.41% on Nov. 20 and traded at $2.84, according to TradingView data. In early October, the token was trading near $6, and it has lost about half of its value since then.

According to recent reports, over the same period, the volume of NEAR Intents went up. "NEAR went from $6 to $3 in about a month. funny thing is, NEAR Intents is doing more volume now than it did in october," NEAR ecosystem contributor Evgeny Haenko wrote on X on Nov. 20.

According to Haenko, NEAR Intents averaged around $129 million in daily volume in October, and in November it was processing around $134 million a day. "The price got cut in half, the business didn't slow down at all. hard for me to be bearish here," he wrote.

According to recent reports, NEAR Intents lets users swap assets across more than 30 blockchains, including Bitcoin, Ethereum, Solana and XRP. The service is built into wallets such as Ledger, Trust Wallet and Brave. Over the past year, its trading volume grew 7.1 times to $39.5 billion.

Recent findings suggest that NEAR Intents has collected about $63 million in fees in total, and the network keeps about 29% of that amount. Fees on the NEAR Intents interface, payments from B2B partners and the spread on better-than-market trades accounted for 16.3%, 9.9% and 2.8% of the fees, respectively. Over the last 30 days, the protocol earned about $1.8 million, compared with $2.2 million in October.

Industry observers note that since February 2026, the protocol has used NEAR Intents revenue to buy NEAR on the market. More than 1.84 million NEAR have gone to the buyback wallet so far, and that is 41.6% of all distributed onchain revenue. Base transaction fees on the network are burned in full.

In a recent development, in early November, the NEAR community also voted to cut the maximum annual issuance from 2.5% to 1.6% over two years. The proposal, HSP-029, went through House of Stake, NEAR's governance initiative, and Haenko is one of its participants.

In a recent development, on Sept. 29, Bitwise launched the first U.S. spot NEAR ETF on NYSE Arca under the ticker NRR. Two days later, on Oct. 1, NEAR Intents paused its services after an exploit that cost about $3.8 million, and the team promised to compensate users in full. The exploiter later returned the funds. "The funds from the $3.8M NEAR Intents hack were sent back in full," NEAR Intents general manager Alex Shevchenko said at the time.

#18635. QuantumScape unveils Osprey all-solid-state cell: 1,000 cycles at 1 atm

📅 11 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1591 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Electrek ↗ Open Full Page

QuantumScape unveils Osprey all-solid-state cell: 1,000 cycles at 1 atm

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1591 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that quantumScape (QS) is finally going all-solid-state.
  • That’s a big deal for the sulfide camp, which includes Toyota, Samsung SDI, BYD, and Factorial.
  • Here’s something QuantumScape has rarely spelled out this plainly: its current product isn’t all-solid-state.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that quantumScape (QS) is finally going all-solid-state. Its new Osprey platform swaps the liquid in its cathode for a sulfide solid electrolyte, and the tech giant states the cells have hit 1,000 full cycles to 80% capacity at just one atmosphere of pressure.

That’s a big deal for the sulfide camp, which includes Toyota, Samsung SDI, BYD, and Factorial. Their cells typically need heavy clamping to work. But the white paper behind the announcement reveals these are small, early lab cells, and some headline numbers come with notable conditions.

Here’s something QuantumScape has rarely spelled out this plainly: its current product isn’t all-solid-state.

The latest white paper describes the QSE platform, including the QSE-5 cell it’s shipping as samples from its Eagle Line pilot production in San Jose, as a ceramic separator paired with “a relatively conventional high-nickel NMC cathode and a liquid catholyte.”.

The solid part is the separator. It sits between the cathode and a lithium-metal anode that QuantumScape doesn’t manufacture at all. The cell is built “anode-free,” and lithium plates against the separator during the first charge.

Recent findings suggest that osprey keeps that separator and anode-free design and swaps the liquid in the cathode for a solid sulfide electrolyte. That makes the whole cell solid.

According to recent reports, the interesting part is that QuantumScape hasn’t changed its mind on sulfides. It has spent years arguing that sulfide electrolytes can’t work as separators, and the white paper doubles down, calling their problems “fundamental properties” of the material rather than engineering challenges.

The tech giant lists four challenges: sulfides react with lithium metal, they need high pressure to keep contact with the electrodes, they struggle at room temperature and below, and they can’t handle fast charging with a lithium-metal anode before dendrites form.

The pressure point is the one automakers care about most. QuantumScape illustrates it this way: 20 atm on a single 10 x 24.2 cm cell works out to roughly 5,000 kg of force, about three mid-size cars. Holding that across a pack takes thick steel end plates and tie rods, which add weight, volume, and cost.

Recent findings suggest that and 20 atm is on the generous side. Many sulfide cells in labs run at 30 to 100+ atm (3 to 12 MPa), and some even higher. China’s FAW reported large-format sulfide cells cycling at 5 MPa, or about 50 atm, in September, which was billed as a low-pressure achievement.

So QS’s pitch is simple: keep the sulfide in the cathode, where it’s good at moving lithium ions, and let the QS ceramic separator handle the lithium metal.

QuantumScape published four main data sets:.

According to recent reports, this is the strongest result. A 2-layer cell with a 50 x 65 mm cathode, the same area as QSE-5, ran 1,000 cycles to about 80% capacity. The test used full 1C charge and 1C discharge, 0 to 100% state of charge, 30°C, and 1 atm. The cathode loading was 5.5 mAh/cm², which is in line with commercial EV cells.

It has been revealed that quantumScape notes no other sulfide-based cell has shown this, and Electrek couldn’t find published data that contradicts it. Academic groups have shown sulfide cells running with little or no external pressure, but not for 1,000 full cycles with a sulfide cathode and lithium-metal anode.

But this is a small cell. By our math, two layers at that size come out to roughly 0.3 to 0.4 Ah, compared to about 5 Ah for a QSE-5.

The press release states “five-minute fast charging from 10% to 80%.” The white paper shows that was achieved at 10C, in a 2-layer cell, at 80°C (176°F). The chart itself is captioned “High temperature enables 5 min fast charge.”.

Industry observers note that batteries charge much faster when hot, and EVs do precondition packs before fast charging. Still, 80°C is well above what EV packs are usually preconditioned to before a fast charge. QS didn’t publish a room-temperature fast-charge result.

“Operational down to -20°C” came from a single-layer cell with a 21 x 21 mm cathode, discharged slowly at C/3. It kept 68% of its room-temperature capacity at -20°C (about 52% of its energy) and 85% at 0°C.

Sources indicate that that’s a real result for a sulfide system, which have historically needed heat. But it’s a tiny cell at a gentle rate.

It has been revealed that the “up to ~1,100 Wh/L” figure is a projection. QS notes high-loading cathodes (10 mAh/cm², about double today’s EV cells) are possible with sulfide catholytes. The test backing that up used an 11 mm coin-size cell at 3 atm, not 1 atm, and ran for 100 cycles.

For reference, QSE-5 is rated at 844 Wh/L and 301 Wh/kg.

The business model is the bigger story.

In a recent development, quantumScape is pitching Osprey as an “open platform.” Customers can use QS’s own sulfide cathode, made with a proprietary dry process, or bring their own. QS indicates it has already tested Osprey with solid cathodes developed by its automotive customers.

In other words, after years of being the sulfide skeptic, QuantumScape now wants to sell its separator and anode-free design to the companies that have spent billions developing sulfide cathodes.

That fits the licensing model it already uses with Volkswagen’s PowerCo and Honda. QS reported $9.8 million in customer billings in Q3 and announced a 100 MWh production line targeting start of production in 2028 for QSE-5.

There’s no timeline for Osprey. The white paper says the process has been demonstrated “at laboratory scale,” that higher-throughput processes are “in the development stage,” and that “significant work remains in process engineering.” Automakers also want larger prismatic cells than QSE-5, which means more layers and more area per layer.

Sources indicate that everyone else is on the clock. Samsung SDI is targeting mass production of sulfide all-solid-state cells in its Ulsan plant in the second half of 2027. BYD plans small-batch sulfide solid-state production in 2027, with mass production toward the end of the decade. Toyota is aiming for 2027 to 2028, after slipping from 2020, 2023, and 2026. Factorial’s sulfide Solstice platform is targeting up to 450 Wh/kg.

CATL, the world’s largest battery maker, remarked in June that true mass-market solid-state is still “years away,” around 2030.

None of those companies has published 1,000-cycle data at 1 atm with a sulfide cathode and lithium-metal anode. That’s QuantumScape’s opening shot.

Recent findings suggest that this is the most interesting thing QuantumScape has published in a while. The numbers are good, but the strategy shift probably stands out most.

In a recent development, the cycle-life result is legit. A 2-layer cell with commercial-area electrodes and realistic loading doing 1,000 full 1C cycles at 1 atm and 30°C is the kind of data the industry hasn’t shown. And QS published the test conditions, which is more than many of its competitors do.

Industry observers note that key thing to remember is that this is a lab test cell. There's a long road ahead to mass manufacturing.

Sources indicate that also, when it hopefully hits the market it will be an incremental improvement, not a quantum leap. Current cells are already in the market doing things like 5 minute charging.

Recent findings suggest that but you can argue the press release oversells what’s in the white paper. A 5-minute charge at 80°C isn’t the same thing as a 5-minute charge, and the release should have said so. The energy density is projected, the cold-weather result is from a cell the size of a postage stamp, and 80% after 1,000 cycles is well below the 95% after 1,000 cycles PowerCo confirmed in QSE’s early cells back in 2024. Different chemistry, different stage, but something worth keeping in mind.

So QuantumScape is essentially admitting the liquid catholyte in QSE isn’t the end game, and that the industry’s massive sulfide investment is something to plug into rather than fight. If your separator is the one part everyone else can’t make work, selling it to them is smart.

The question is time. QS is still scaling QSE-5, with a 100 MWh line not due until 2028. Osprey is a lab process. Will anyone in the sulfide camp license it before their own 2027 to 2030 production intends lock in? At this point, it sounds like this is QS’ bet right now.

Industry News: Enjin Matrixchain Votes on OpenGov Today: What Changes for ENJ Holders on November 16

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1537 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nulltx

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, enjin holders vote through November 13 on moving Matrixchain to OpenGov on November 16.
  • Enjin's fresh proposal deposit sounds steep at 1,000 ENJ.
  • Enjin holders have until today, November 13, to vote on moving the Matrixchain to the Fort Canning release.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

In a recent development, enjin holders vote through November 13 on moving Matrixchain to OpenGov on November 16. Here is how the nine tracks, the 1,000 ENJ deposit and conviction voting work, and what the Relaychain vote highlights.

Enjin's fresh proposal deposit sounds steep at 1,000 ENJ. It's actually the cheap part.

Enjin holders have until today, November 13, to vote on moving the Matrixchain to the Fort Canning release. The referendum opened November 10. If it passes, the upgrade is targeted for November 16 at block #12,319,600, with the network moving from runtime 1.3.1 to 1.4.3. Enjin's Fort Canning announcement lays out the blueprint, and the official changelog carries the technical detail.

Sources indicate that the Relaychain has already made the jump. Referendum #16 approved its upgrade on October 28, and it went live on November 9. The Matrixchain vote is the second half of one upgrade, and it is the half that changes how Matrixchain makes decisions from then on.

According to recent reports, early coverage reported the schedule and the headline numbers: nine tracks, 1,000 ENJ. The changelog and the governance portal show the mechanics behind them, and those mechanics change more than the headlines suggest.

Sources indicate that today, the Matrixchain runs its governance through the older Democracy, Council and Technical Committee pallets, the modules that handle proposals and votes. Fort Canning replaces all three with a new set: Referenda, Conviction Voting, Origins, Whitelist and the Enjin Fellowship. Under OpenGov, any account can submit a referendum on one of nine tracks, and from the moment the upgrade lands, Matrixchain's own upgrades go through that process.

A track is a lane for a particular kind of decision. Enjin's changelog describes the families: Root and the admin tracks for the highest-stakes changes, Whitelisted Caller for proposals the Fellowship fast-tracks, and two special tracks, Referendum Killer and Referendum Canceller, for stopping a proposal that shouldn't proceed. Matrixchain gets no treasury tracks: those, sized by how much a proposal would spend, stay on the Relaychain, where treasury requests now go. Each track has its own deposit, approval curve and enactment period, and the Enjin Fellowship can fast-track time-sensitive proposals.

Splitting decisions this way means a small treasury request doesn't face the same bar as a change to the chain's core. Riskier tracks demand larger deposits and more support, while smaller ones move faster and cost less.

The submission deposit rises from 0.025 ENJ to 1,000 ENJ on every track, a 40,000-fold increase. The deposit is refunded when a referendum passes or is canceled, and it exists to deter spam. As an illustration, using the roughly $66 million market cap reported in early October, ENJ traded near three cents, which would put 1,000 ENJ around $33.

It has been revealed that that is only the entry ticket. The cost that matters comes next. A referendum also needs a decision deposit before it moves into voting, and the changelog lists steep figures: 2,500,000 ENJ on Root and Fellowship Admin, 1,000,000 ENJ on the other admin tracks, and 2,500 to 250,000 ENJ on the Relaychain's treasury tracks. At the same illustrative price, the 2.5 million ENJ Root deposit comes to roughly $80,000, about 0.12% of the 2.02 billion ENJ total issuance.

Recent findings suggest that so proposing is cheap, and pushing a proposal through is not. Anyone can raise an idea, but anyone who wants the network to vote on something major needs real stake in the outcome. The changelog says the same values apply on both chains, and Matrixchain adopts them for its fresh tracks.

It has been revealed that the best evidence of how these votes work comes from the Relaychain referendum that has already finished. Enjin's governance portal shows referendum #16 as finalised, approved on October 28 and enacted on November 9.

The final tally on the page is small. Eleven voters cast 381,303.02 ENJ of conviction-weighted voting power, and all of it went to Aye: 100% in favor, 0 ENJ against. The page also highlights raw, unweighted support of 271,303.2 ENJ, which it describes as the total balance backing the proposal and the figure the support curve uses. The conviction multiplier on the page runs from under 1x up to 6x.

Two numbers stand out. First, an entire chain upgrade passed with 271,303 ENJ of raw support, about 0.013% of the 2.02 billion ENJ total issuance, a figure worked out from the portal's number. Second, conviction added about 110,000 ENJ of weight on top of the raw balance, an average multiplier of roughly 1.4x. Voters picked up some extra weight, but most didn't lock their tokens for the long periods that earn the top multipliers.

It has been revealed that A 100% Aye result indicates little by itself. A scheduled upgrade with no organized opposition passes easily, and the tally highlights how thin engagement was.

Fort Canning adds the safeguard that thin turnout calls for. A referendum now needs a minimum share of total ENJ voting in support. The changelog sets 0.5% on Root and the admin tracks, 0.005% to 0.125% on the Relaychain's treasury tracks, 0.1% for Referendum Killer and 0.05% for Referendum Canceller. Measured against 2.02 billion ENJ, that means about 10.1 million ENJ on Root, roughly 101,000 to 2.5 million on the treasury tracks, about 2.02 million to kill a referendum and about 1.01 million to cancel one.

Referendum #16's 271,303 ENJ of raw support would clear the lowest treasury floor of about 101,000 ENJ, but it would miss the Root floor by a factor of about 37. The page doesn't show which track the referendum used, and a runtime upgrade typically sits on a high-stakes track, so the Root comparison works as an illustration and not as a finding. The floors also didn't exist when #16 passed, since Fort Canning introduced them.

It has been revealed that that is the real change. Under the upcoming rules, 11 wallets can't carry a chain-level decision on their own. Low turnout means failure, and proposals that matter will need far more ENJ behind them. Enjin's changelog says Matrixchain upgrades go through OpenGov starting with this one, which suggests today's vote still runs on the current system, so the floors will first bite on the first OpenGov referendum.

In a recent development, holders who haven't voted can still do so through Enjin's governance portal before the window closes. Voting locks tokens, so the lock length is worth checking first. Enjin's support article on voting explains the trade-off: the longer the lock, the more a vote counts, and tokens stay locked until the period ends.

In a recent development, node operators on the Matrixchain can wait for the result before upgrading, as Enjin has indicated, and then follow the changelog for the version to install. Relaychain operators already needed client version 1.8.1.

This vote is more about control than speed. OpenGov spreads decisions across tracks with deposits and support floors built for the weight of each choice, and it moves ENJ holders from voting on a handful of items to a standing governance system. The Relaychain's first vote indicated how little participation it took under the old rules, and the first referenda after November 16 will show whether holders turn out for the newly introduced ones. If most proposals stall at the decision deposit, the system costs too much. If they clear with a handful of voters, the floors aren't doing their job. Either result will tell holders what their ENJ can do.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Famous financial educator and author of "Rich Dad Poor Dad" Robert Kiyosaki has disclosed when investors should begin accumulating Bitcoin (BTC) during the current cryptocurrency market bloodbath.
  • While he is consistently bullish on Bitcoin, Kiyosaki is asking investors to be patient and not buy the flagship cryptocurrency before the current crash ends.
  • 20, Kiyosaki shared an vital investment lesson and warned his followers against catching a falling knife.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Famous financial educator and author of "Rich Dad Poor Dad" Robert Kiyosaki has disclosed when investors should begin accumulating Bitcoin (BTC) during the current cryptocurrency market bloodbath.

While he is consistently bullish on Bitcoin, Kiyosaki is asking investors to be patient and not buy the flagship cryptocurrency before the current crash ends.

In his latest X post on Nov. 20, Kiyosaki shared an vital investment lesson and warned his followers against catching a falling knife.

"Never grab a falling knife," Kiyosaki warned.

The financial guru suggested that this means investors should wait until the cryptocurrency market crash ends before buying more Bitcoin.

"That means wait for the crash to end….before buying," Kiyosaki elaborated.

Notably, Kiyosaki shared that he began buying Bitcoin when its price was around $20,000 after another major market crash.

The best-selling author hinted that he is planning to do the same during the current market downturn.

"Will wait for Bitcoin bottom again," Kiyosaki noted.

The financial educator reminded his followers of one of his notable investment tips.

"Your profit is made when you buy….not when you sell," Kiyosaki noted.

Basically, the financial educator suggested that investors should prioritize finding good entry prices rather than trying to buy Bitcoin while its price keeps dropping.

However, Kiyosaki did not specify a Bitcoin price target or how he is going to know that the market has bottomed out.

Kiyosaki's remarks follow another devastating Bitcoin crash that took the flagship cryptocurrency to its lowest level in more than four months.

Sources indicate that on Nov. 20, the world's largest cryptocurrency crashed below the key psychological price level of $60,000 for the first time since July.

According to Reuters, Bitcoin crashed to around $59,381. Bitcoin shed over 3% in a single trading session.

Interestingly, BlackRock's iShares Bitcoin Trust (IBIT) saw a record $541.1 million in daily outflows.

  • After unveiling the GV90 at the Palace of Fine Arts in San Francisco in August (which we had the pleasure to see firsthand), Genesis rolled out the new “ultra-luxe” SUV in its home market of Korea on Tuesday.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that genesis opened orders for the ultra-luxury electric SUV in South Korea, with prices starting at over $100,000. If you want coach doors, however, it will cost you a bit more.

Hyundai’s luxury brand is moving upscale with the GV90, its first fully electric three-row flagship SUV.

After unveiling the GV90 at the Palace of Fine Arts in San Francisco in August (which we had the pleasure to see firsthand), Genesis rolled out the new “ultra-luxe” SUV in its home market of Korea on Tuesday.

The Genesis GV90 introduces several “world-first” innovations, including the first independently opening and closing B-pillarless coach doors, a 12-airbag roof airbag system, and genuine wood floors with radiant heating.

It’s available in two models: the GV90 Standard with traditional swing doors and the GV90 Neolun, which features the “Neolun Arch Gate,” Genesis’ hidden B-pillar coach door system.

In Korea, the Genesis GV90 Standard 7-seater model starts at 139.5 million won, or about $104,000.

The GV90 Individual Lounge Seat (6-seater) starts at 145.5 million won ($108,500); the GV90 Neolun Standard (6-seater) starts at 189.9 million won ($141,500), while the top-spec GV90 Neolun Executive Suite (4-seater) starts at 239.5 million won ($178,500).

Based on Hyundai’s new eMP platform, developed exclusively for its flagships, Genesis noted the GV90 is like a “moving private lounge,” complete with a multi-chamber air suspension and a dual electronic limited-slip differential (E-LSD).

The platform is designed to open up interior space for the B-pillarless coach doors, swivel seats, and more.

When parked, the front seats swivel a full 180 degrees to face rear passengers or to create what Genesis calls “a face-to-face lounge-like configuration.”.

The interior is about as over-the-top as you could expect, with massive digital screens, premium materials, and plenty of luxury extras.

The GV90 is the first Hyundai Motor Group vehicle to feature its new extendable display and the first Genesis model equipped with its next-gen Pleos Connect infotainment system.

Together, they create what Genesis calls a newly introduced realm of “display expandability.” While other vehicles, like the new Tucson and IONIQ 3, also use Pleos Connect, Hyundai developed an exclusive version for the GV90.

When the vehicle is parked, the screen can expand to 24.6″ at the push of a button, transforming it into a massive Cinematic Display.

Once extended, the display switches to Media Home mode, where you can watch Netflix, live TV, stream music, and more with third-party apps.

A mobile private theater wouldn’t be complete without a premium audio system, right? To top it off, Genesis added a 25-speaker Bang & Olufsen Premier 3D Sound System with Dolby Atmos, so it sounds like you’re actually at the movies.

In place of a traditional instrument cluster, the GV90 has a 25″ Head-Up Display (HUD) that demonstrates the vehicle’s speed, navigation directions, and other ADAS functions directly on the windshield.

Recent findings suggest that the GV90 is also the first Hyundai Motor Group vehicle with a buttonless power system. When you enter the vehicle and close the door, the Motion Column Shifter moves from the 12 o’clock position to the 2 o’clock position.

Meanwhile, the Crystal Sphere between the driver and passenger rotates to indicate it’s ready to drive. The vehicle starts when you press the brake.

As a full-size flagship SUV, the Genesis GV90 is massive. It measures 208.1″ (5,285 mm) long, 79.9″ (2,030 mm) wide, and 71.5″ (1,815 mm) tall (71.4″ with 24″ tires), with a 127.8″ (3,245 mm) wheelbase.

That’s even bigger than the Hyundai IONIQ 9 (199.2″/5,060 mm in length) and Kia EV9 (197.4″/5,010 mm).

According to recent reports, to power a full-size flagship SUV, it needs a big battery. The GV90 uses a 123.5 kWh battery, the largest among Hyundai Motor’s EVs, which Genesis stated provides a driving range of 500 km (310 miles) for the 7-seater version with 22″ wheels.

The GV90 Neonlun 6-seater with 24″ wheels has a range of up to 460 km (286 miles) on a single charge.

It’s equipped with a upcoming dual-motor all-wheel-drive (AWD) system that delivers a combined 657 hp (490 kW) and 590 lb-ft (800 Nm) of torque, making it Hyundai Motor Group’s most powerful electric vehicle.

When using a 350 kW fast charger, the vehicle’s battery can recharge from 10% to 80% in about 22 minutes.

Sources indicate that and.... once again Hyundai shortchanges the range. If you are going to drop a 200+ inch premium upright SUV into the market it requires a 140+ kwh battery (Rivian, BMW) to deliver segment appropriate range. You do not have to jump to a 200 kwh Escalade (though it is probably a better buy in every respect) but at least deliver 140+. Also, memo to powertrain engineering group: 350 kw is getting outdated on fast charging especially on a vehicle of this size. And while I am at it, what happened to the promised L3 ADAS? I think the 2028 Caddy is worth the wait compared to this.

“Thanks to the enthusiastic interest and support for the GV90 since its global premiere, we have begun full-scale sales in Korea first,” a Genesis official said, adding the flagship SUV will “set a new standard for luxury.”.

Following Korea, Genesis is expected to launch the GV90 in the US and other global markets in early 2027.

Industry observers note that genesis has yet to reveal US prices, but the GV90 Standard model is expected to start at around $100,000. The GV90 Neolun, on the other hand, will likely start closer to $150,000 or more.

Sources indicate that what do you think of the flagship Genesis GV90? Would you buy the standard version for about $100,000 or pay the extra for the Neolun with coach doors? Let us know in the comments.

"People are taking liquidity out of a very liquid market, crypto included — Bitcoin, XRP — and moving it into SpaceX. The exact same thing happened coming into the Anthropic IPO," he said. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Charles Hoskinson’s Cardano-linked privacy blockchain Midnight has inked a big initial deal with a Japanese payments company as it aims to make further inroads into traditional finance.

The news comes soon after a key breakthrough for Midnight in the United Kingdom, where Monument Bank started tokenizing customer deposits on the blockchain.

Per a Nov. 19 NADA NEWS report, Midnight Foundation President Fahmi Syed said the foundation had inked an MOU (memorandum of understanding) with a major Japanese payments company.

Industry observers note that syed did not name the manufacturer. But the deal is a major one for Midnight’s bid to establish a presence in Japan’s financial services sector.

However, it is just an initial agreement, and no commercial services have been rolled out in Japan yet.

It is also worth noting that the Midnight Foundation is talking to some major Japanese banks and companies working with intellectual property and medical data.

According to Syed, he spent two days in Tokyo meeting with major financial institutions and other companies.

Japan has been a key market for Midnight, along with the United States.

According to Midnight Foundation Japan country manager Taro Kimura, Japan is the only Asian country where the foundation has a local representative on the ground.

Midnight has been eyeing Japan more keenly due to the country’s sizeable Cardano community.

The Japanese push comes hot on the heels of a historic development in the British banking sector.

Industry observers note that on Nov. 18, British financial institution Monument Bank started tokenizing retail customer deposits on Midnight. It is the first UK bank to launch such a product on a public blockchain.

In a recent development, the first phase of the venture involves up to £250 million in tokenized deposits. For this, the bank is offering customers a 12-month fixed annual interest rate of 5.2%.

Sources indicate that midnight employs zero-knowledge cryptography to safeguard sensitive transaction details, unlike traditional public blockchains. As a result, banks can meet compliance requirements while keeping their customers’ private information and transaction details out of public view.

Porsche CEO takes a shot at Tesla’s ‘flying’ Roadster stunt show

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (881 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Tesla’s “flying” Roadster just took a hit from Porsche.
  • Both automakers revealed their next halo cars on the same day, October 15.
  • According to recent reports, tesla finally unveiled the next-gen Roadster last month, almost nine years after the 2017 prototype.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tesla’s “flying” Roadster just took a hit from Porsche. Speaking at a conference in Berlin today, CEO Michael Leiters said Porsche wants “to completely steer clear from any kind of effects and highlights,” according to Bloomberg.

Both automakers revealed their next halo cars on the same day, October 15. Tesla made a Roadster flip in mid-air. Porsche showed the Mission S, and Leiters says the two cars aren’t even chasing the same customers.

According to recent reports, tesla finally unveiled the next-gen Roadster last month, almost nine years after the 2017 prototype. The main event was a car using compressed-air thrusters to launch off a ramp, rotate in the air, and come back down on its wheels.

Recent findings suggest that it was the payoff for months of hype. Musk spent most of the year promising a “flying” Roadster demo, and it slipped more than once. We reported in June that it had been pushed to August to make room for SpaceX thruster work.

There are three versions. The Performance trim uses suction fans and claims 0-60 mph in under 1.6 seconds, the Thrust trim adds rear cold-gas thrusters for a claimed sub-0.9-second run, and the single-seat Rocket trim gets thrusters all around the car and isn’t approved for public roads. Tesla gave no price and no production date, just Musk’s “2028, actually.”.

It has been revealed that porsche went the other way. Under the skin, the Mission S can take either a hybrid or a straight combustion powertrain. It’s a mid-engine car that sits above the 911 in the lineup, and well above it in price.

Leiters said customer response has been “overwhelming” and that Porsche would rather show off real technical innovation than put on a show. If it reaches production, Ferrari is the obvious target, and Porsche hasn’t played in that segment since the 918 Spyder. Porsche is counting on a pricier, more exclusive lineup to rebuild its profits.

It has been revealed that not everyone in the supercar world agrees with Leiters. Ferrari CEO Benedetto Vigna rated Tesla’s Roadster launch “10 out of 10” last month.

Leiters has a point, even if Porsche pitching a gas and hybrid supercar as “technical innovation” in 2026 is a bit rich. But what bothers me more is who Tesla is aiming at.

I’m concerned Tesla is starting to appeal to the lowest common denominator: people who watch a Roadster hop off a ramp and believe an actual flying car is coming. Musk pushed that idea himself. On Joe Rogan’s show, he called the upcoming demo “unforgettable” and mentioned that if Peter Thiel wants a flying car, “we should be able to buy one.”.

That’s not real. Cold-gas thrusters work like a giant can of compressed air, and the math is brutal. The Rocket trim carries 400 liters of air at 10,000 psi, roughly 200 kg of gas. At the roughly 80 kN its rear thrusters produce, even a very efficient nozzle empties that tank in a few seconds. Then refilling it takes six to seven hours.

Also someone on Bluesky pointed out that the video shows Mach diamonds in the exhaust stream of the thrusters. Which means it's so loud that anyone within 100 feet would suffer immediate and permanent hearing loss. This Roadster isn't useful for anything other than temporarily pumping stock prices.

Industry observers note that so the Roadster’s “flying” will always be limited to stunts like this one. No hopping over traffic. No hovering. A couple of seconds of air, then a long wait at a compressor.

Sources indicate that that’s great for a viral clip. But this is a car that dropped from a promised 620 miles of range in 2017 to “over 300” today, and Tesla would rather sell people on a flight the physics can’t deliver.

It’s hard for me to get excited for that. As a BEV enthusiast, I’m not more excited about Porsche’s ICE Mission S, but at least I trust Porsche to actually deliver that to customers.

#18616. Tech Report: MIT Review Acclaims zk-SNARKs, but zk-STARKs May Steal the Show

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1240 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Nulltx ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: MIT Review Acclaims zk-SNARKs, but zk-STARKs May Steal the Show

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1240 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nulltx

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Updated look back: this article revisits a 2018 story with what has happened since.
  • According to recent reports, in February 2018, MIT Technology Review put zero-knowledge proofs on its list of 10 Breakthrough Technologies under the title "Perfect Online Privacy", and singled out zk-SNARKs as the practical version.
  • Recent findings suggest that the short version: STARKs took a large share of the stage, SNARKs adapted, and Bulletproofs found a narrower job.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Updated look back: this article revisits a 2018 story with what has happened since.

According to recent reports, in February 2018, MIT Technology Review put zero-knowledge proofs on its list of 10 Breakthrough Technologies under the title "Perfect Online Privacy", and singled out zk-SNARKs as the practical version. zk-STARKs, published a few weeks earlier, did not replace SNARKs, but they fixed the two weaknesses MIT pointed at and now secure a major Ethereum scaling network.

Recent findings suggest that the short version: STARKs took a large share of the stage, SNARKs adapted, and Bulletproofs found a narrower job. Here is how the three compare and how the story played out.

A zero-knowledge proof lets you prove that a statement is true without showing the data behind it. MIT's examples were proving you are over 18 without giving your birth date, or proving you can afford a payment without showing your balance.

According to recent reports, the idea is old. According to ethereum.org, it first appeared in a 1985 paper. What changed was that it became usable. MIT's entry, written by Mike Orcutt, credited much of that progress to Zcash, a currency debuted in late 2016, and listed Zcash, JPMorgan Chase and ING as key players.

The same entry named two drawbacks. zk-SNARKs were slow and heavy to compute, and they needed a "trusted setup". It added that researchers were already looking for alternatives without those problems, but did not name any.

zk-SNARK stands for zero-knowledge succinct non-interactive argument of knowledge. "Succinct" is the selling point. Zcash's documentation states a proof is only a few hundred bytes and can be checked in a few milliseconds, even for a very large computation.

That is what makes shielded Zcash transactions possible. The transaction is encrypted on the blockchain, yet the network can still confirm that it follows the rules.

Recent findings suggest that the cost is the setup. Early SNARKs needed a one-time ceremony that produced public parameters. The ceremony also produced secret randomness, and Zcash's own documentation says anyone who kept it could forge proofs and create counterfeit coins. Zcash ran two multi-party ceremonies, one for its Sprout version and one for Sapling, so that no single person held the secret. Customers still had to trust that at least one participant destroyed their share.

Sources indicate that the STARK paper, "Scalable, transparent, and post-quantum secure computational integrity", was submitted to the IACR ePrint archive on January 10, 2018 by Eli Ben-Sasson, Iddo Bentov, Yinon Horesh and Michael Riabzev. Its title states the three goals.

According to recent reports, transparent means no trusted setup. STARKs use public randomness, so there is no secret to leak.

Recent findings suggest that post-quantum refers to the underlying math. Ethereum.org explains that SNARKs depend on elliptic curve cryptography, which a future quantum computer may break, while STARKs rely only on collision-resistant hash functions.

Scalable means the work of checking a proof grows far more slowly than the computation being proved.

According to recent reports, the trade-off is size. STARK proofs are larger, and ethereum.org notes that this makes them more expensive to verify on Ethereum. Figures quoted in the Ethereum Stack Exchange thread that cites this article give a sense of scale: about 288 bytes for a SNARK against about 45,000 bytes for a STARK in one comparison, and "hundreds of kilobytes" in one developer's real project. Those numbers depend heavily on the computation, so treat them as orders of magnitude.

Bulletproofs came out of Stanford in 2017, from Benedikt Bünz, Jonathan Bootle, Dan Boneh, Andrew Poelstra, Pieter Wuille and Greg Maxwell. Like STARKs, they need no trusted setup.

According to recent reports, they were designed for one job: proving that a hidden amount in a confidential transaction falls within a valid range. The Stanford project page states they cut that proof from over 10 kB to under 1 kB. It also says a Bulletproof takes longer to verify than a SNARK, which is why they are not used for proving large computations.

Monero added Bulletproofs in its October 2018 network upgrade. Its documentation reports that average transaction size fell by at least 80 percent.

In a recent development, partly. Three things happened after 2018.

STARKs reached production. Eli Ben-Sasson, the paper's first author, co-founded StarkWare with Alessandro Chiesa and Uri Kolodny. The organization used STARKs first in StarkEx, a scaling service for individual clients, and then in Starknet, which introduced its Alpha on Ethereum mainnet in November 2021. Starknet's documentation describes it as a permissionless validity rollup that settles on Ethereum using STARK proofs.

Zero-knowledge moved from privacy to scaling. MIT framed the technology as a privacy tool. Its largest use on Ethereum became zk-rollups, which process transactions off-chain and post one proof that they were all valid. Ethereum.org lists Starknet alongside ZKsync, Scroll, Linea, Polygon zkEVM and others. Ethereum.org also puts the cost of verifying a single SNARK on Ethereum at about 500,000 gas and says STARKs cost more, which keeps small proofs attractive.

SNARKs fixed their own weakness. PLONK, published in August 2019 by Ariel Gabizon, Zachary Williamson and Oana Ciobotaru, is a universal SNARK: one setup can serve many different programs instead of one ceremony per program. Halo went further. Zcash claims Halo removes the trusted setup entirely, and its Orchard shielded protocol, activated with the NU5 upgrade in May 2022, runs on the Halo 2 proving system.

In a recent development, that last point matters for the old "SNARKs need a trusted setup" comparison. It was accurate in 2018. It no longer holds for every SNARK.

Industry observers note that the fair verdict: STARKs did not push SNARKs aside, but they did prove that transparency and hash-based security work at scale. The choice today is less about which family wins and more about what you need: the smallest proof, no setup, or protection against quantum attacks.

Latest Update: Toyota and Subaru hit the ‘sweet spot’ with affordable electric SUVs

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (733 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Toyota and Subaru’s fresh electric SUVs are catching on with buyers, offering various options and prices ranging from about $35,000 to $45,000, or the “sweet spot” of the US market.
  • The US electric vehicle market rebounded in the third quarter with 262,649 EVs sold, according to Kelley Blue Book estimates, up 6.1% from Q2 and the strongest performance of the year.
  • Although nearly every automaker has sold fewer EVs so far this year than in the same period in 2025, as buyers rushed to claim the $7,500 tax credit before it expired, a handful of brands are seeing considerably higher demand.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Toyota and Subaru’s fresh electric SUVs are catching on with buyers, offering various options and prices ranging from about $35,000 to $45,000, or the “sweet spot” of the US market.

The US electric vehicle market rebounded in the third quarter with 262,649 EVs sold, according to Kelley Blue Book estimates, up 6.1% from Q2 and the strongest performance of the year.

Although nearly every automaker has sold fewer EVs so far this year than in the same period in 2025, as buyers rushed to claim the $7,500 tax credit before it expired, a handful of brands are seeing considerably higher demand.

Outside of Rivian, Toyota and Subaru are the only brands that have higher year-over-year EV sales in the US through the third quarter.

Combined, Toyota and Subaru have sold nearly 50,000 EVs through the first nine months of 2026, more than double compared to the same period last year.

Toyota alone has sold nearly 35,000 electric vehicles, up 183.4% YOY, while Subaru sold 14,630, up 46.7%. And that’s not even including the additional 12,676 sold under the Lexus brand, up 137.4% YOY.

While the two Japanese automakers were infamously slow to transition to battery electric vehicles, the timing worked in their favor.

After launching the heavily updated bZ in late 2025, previously called the bZ4X, Toyota’s electric SUV suddenly became one of America’s most popular EVs. Through Q3, it was the fourth best-selling EV in the US, trailing only the Hyundai IONIQ 5, Tesla Model 3, and Tesla Model Y.

It has been revealed that starting at $35,000, the Toyota bZ is one of the most affordable EVs in the US. It also offers up to 314 miles of range in the FWD Plus trim, which starts at $37,980.

Toyota and Subaru now each sell three electric SUVs, which share the same platform and technology.

With prices ranging from roughly $35,000 to about $45,000, Stephanie Valdez Streaty, director of industry insights at Cox Automotive, noted (via Bloomberg) Toyota and Subaru’s new EVs are affordable and hit the “sweet spot” of the US car market.

Toyota also sells the smaller, sporty C-HR, starting at $37,080, and the larger, more rugged bZ Woodland, which starts at $45,380.

Subaru, on the other hand, sells the updated Solterra ($38,495, plus the smaller Uncharted ($34,995) and midsize Trailseeker ($39,995).

Karla Fisher, a Marine and retired engineer, told Bloomberg that the Subaru Trailseeker was her “most favorite car of all time.”.

Sources indicate that while she considered buying an EV before the $7,500 federal credit expired last September, none met her requirements at the time. Fisher wanted at least 7″ of ground clearance, 250 miles or more range, and a price that was similar, or even less than a comparible gas-powered vehicle.

The Subaru Trailseeker offers all of that and starts at under $40,000. Toyota and Subaru’s electric SUVs all start at about $45,000 or less, which is even less than the average new vehicle.

According to the latest Kelley Blue Book figures, the average price for a latest vehicle in the US reached a record $51,109 in October, up 2.1% YOY.

Great as these may be, there is little inventory to be found.

There are less than 500 Uncharted available Nationwide.

You can't sell what you don't have. Yes, they can be ordered for sure, but how many missed sales does that model create?

In a recent development, subaru spokesperson Dominick Infante said the affordable EV prices are mainly thanks to its partnership with Toyota. “We do believe there’s an EV future,” Infante added.

Next year, both brands will add a three-row electric SUV with the Toyota Highlander EV and Subaru Getaway.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, italy’s largest banking group, Intesa Sanpaolo, increased its spot altcoin ETF holdings according to a upcoming disclosure.
  • Industry observers note that the bank’s disclosed crypto ETF holdings grew in Q3 2026 to $108.56 million, up $17 million, while digital asset prices moved sideways.
  • Bitcoin, the largest asset in the portfolio, was reduced to make room for altcoins in a possible bid to diversify assets.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, italy’s largest banking group, Intesa Sanpaolo, increased its spot altcoin ETF holdings according to a upcoming disclosure. This follows capital rotation out of Bitcoin products by a slew of traditional firms amid dwindling market sentiment.

Industry observers note that the bank’s disclosed crypto ETF holdings grew in Q3 2026 to $108.56 million, up $17 million, while digital asset prices moved sideways. In June, total assets were worth $90 million as it looked to diversify and grow holdings systematically.

Bitcoin, the largest asset in the portfolio, was reduced to make room for altcoins in a possible bid to diversify assets. At the end of Q2, BTC holdings stood at $69.32 million but dropped slightly to above $61 million last quarter. The firm’s Ethereum exposure also dropped to $5 million.

However, Solana and XRP products filled the vacuum, highlighting institutional appetite for these assets. At the time of writing, the bank’s spot Solana ETF exposure is at $14.1 million after its investment in the Bitwise Solana Staking ETF ballooned from seven shares to 875,407 shares.

Intesa’s XRP investment also grew over the same period to $27.2 million, driven mainly by 402,750 shares in the Bitwise XRP ETF. The tech giant’s shares in the Grayscale XRP Trust ETF remained unchanged across both quarters.

Industry observers note that more broadly, the bank reduced its Bitcoin ETF exposure and increased SOL and XRP products. Most experts believe it follows the current market trend, and firms, especially traditional companies, need to diversify to make up for Bitcoin’s decline.

Historically, during bear phases, there’s a huge rotation of capital into altcoins, though it’s not sustained for long. As expected, Solana and XRP become institutional favorites, while Ethereum trades similarly to Bitcoin.

According to recent reports, the former have the potential to record spikes within the red wave, like in 2022 before the approval of spot ETF products in the United States. These products opened up digital assets to a new stash of traditional capital.

Sources indicate that intesa and other banks have since increased their crypto exposure, driven by the need to diversify assets and a broader adoption spree. Heightened institutional and retail interests pushed Bitcoin to an all-time high above $125k last year. At the moment, BTC trades at $63,819, while Ethereum is slightly below $1,800.
